title: HIGH: compact()/vacuum() never invalidate the lazy int8/4-bit quantization caches — two-pass search then scores the WRONG rows, or panics
description:
Found by user-directed semantic-path review (MossyPine, 2026-07-31). CONFIRMED at origin/main index/src/lib.rs:2843-2861 (fields :784, :790; consumers search.rs:850-859, :988-998).

DEFECT: rewrite_index reassigns self.data, self.metadata, all three offsets and self.wal_entries — but vectors_i8: OnceLock<Vec<i8>> and vectors_nibbles: OnceLock<Vec<u8>> are NEVER reset. They appear only at :784/:790 and the three constructors (:1573/:1785); search.rs:851 and :989 are pure get_or_init, so a slab built before the rewrite is reused against completely different backing bytes.

FAILURE A (silent wrong results): search_top_k_int8_two_pass builds the slab for N rows; soft_delete(); vacuum() (:2287 -> rewrite_index) leaves N-1 rows and swaps self.data while the slab still holds the old N. The next two-pass search scores pass-1 candidates from the WRONG DOCUMENTS for every row after the first removed tombstone, then pass-2 rescores those wrong candidates exactly — so returned scores look perfectly self-consistent while true top-k members are silently missing.
FAILURE B (panic in a search): compact() (:2596) merges the WAL in, record_count() grows and wal_entries is cleared (:2605), reopening the two-pass gate; int8_scan_range_orig_with_key then slices slab[off..off+dim] past the stale slab's length.

No test exercises a two-pass search after compact/vacuum.

FIX: make both fields RwLock<Option<..>> (or take &mut self and assign OnceLock::new()) and clear them at the end of rewrite_index alongside self.data = reloaded.data.
close_reason: Landed 0a0b7966: rewrite_index now resets vectors_i8/vectors_nibbles OnceLocks in the reload block, so vacuum()/compact() invalidate the lazy quantization slabs. Red-proofed (test fails pre-fix with 'int8 slab served stale pre-vacuum rows', deterministic via runtime row-order discovery + one-hot axes); covers both slabs across vacuum AND compact incl. the grown-region case; 514 index lib tests green; clippy/fmt clean (lint follow-up 2e08930d).

title: Per-Hit Search Result Explanations
description:
Add opt-in per-hit explanations that decompose why each result was ranked where it is. This is the #1 feature request pattern in search libraries — users need to debug "why did this rank higher than that?"

## Background

Frankensearch is a hybrid search system that combines lexical (BM25), semantic (fast and quality embeddings), and reranking signals via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Each result's final score is a composite of 4+ score sources, each with its own normalization and weighting. Debugging relevance issues requires understanding the contribution of each source, but currently there is no way to inspect score decomposition at the per-hit level.

## Design

### Data Structures

```rust
pub struct HitExplanation {
    pub final_score: f64,
    pub components: Vec<ScoreComponent>,
    pub phase: SearchPhase,
    pub rank_movement: Option<RankMovement>,
}

pub struct ScoreComponent {
    pub source: ScoreSource,
    pub raw_score: f64,
    pub normalized_score: f64,
    pub rrf_contribution: f64,
    pub weight: f64,
}

pub enum ScoreSource {
    LexicalBm25 { matched_terms: Vec<String>, tf: f64, idf: f64 },
    SemanticFast { embedder: String, cosine_sim: f64 },
    SemanticQuality { embedder: String, cosine_sim: f64 },
    Rerank { model: String, logit: f64, sigmoid: f64 },
}

pub struct RankMovement {
    pub initial_rank: usize,
    pub refined_rank: usize,
    pub delta: i32,
    pub reason: String, // "promoted by quality embedder", "demoted after rerank"
}
```

### Activation

`TwoTierConfig { explain: true, .. }` — when false (default), no allocation overhead. The explain flag gates all explanation-related computation and allocation, ensuring zero cost for production workloads that don't need debugging.

### Integration Points

- **RRF fusion**: record per-source rank and RRF contribution for each hit
- **Score normalization**: record raw -> normalized mapping so users can see how raw scores were transformed
- **Two-tier blend**: record fast vs quality contribution for each hit
- **Rerank**: record pre/post rerank scores and the logit/sigmoid values from the reranker model
- **TwoTierSearcher**: attach HitExplanation to FusedHit when explain=true

## Justification

Debugging search relevance is the hardest part of operating a hybrid search system. Without explanations, users resort to printf debugging across 4+ score sources, manually correlating log lines to understand why a particular document ranked where it did. This makes frankensearch self-documenting at runtime. Every major search engine (Elasticsearch, Lucene, Vespa) provides this feature because it's essential for relevance tuning.

## Considerations

- Memory allocation: when explain=false, zero additional allocations per hit
- Serialization: HitExplanation should implement Serialize for JSON output (debugging tools)
- String formatting: provide a human-readable Display impl for terminal/log output
- Partial explanations: if a score source is not active (e.g., no reranker configured), that component is simply absent from the components list

## Testing

- [ ] Unit: verify explanation components sum to final score (within floating-point epsilon)
- [ ] Unit: verify RankMovement correctly tracks position changes across phases
- [ ] Unit: verify zero overhead when explain=false (benchmark: search with explain=false should show no regression vs current baseline)
- [ ] Unit: verify all ScoreSource variants are correctly populated
- [ ] Integration: full pipeline explanation with all score sources active (BM25 + fast + quality + rerank)
- [ ] Integration: partial pipeline (e.g., only BM25 + fast) produces correct partial explanation
acceptance_criteria:
1. The feature is fully implemented according to this bead design, scope, and referenced files or modules.
2. Integration with dependent components is complete and behavior remains correct across normal and degraded flows.
3. Edge and error cases are explicitly handled with deterministic outcomes and clear reason codes or errors.
4. Unit and integration tests (and e2e where relevant) are added, passing, and include detailed structured logging assertions.
5. Performance and resource expectations in the bead are validated and documented with reproducible evidence.
6. Every explicit checklist item in the bead description is implemented and verified by automated tests or validation commands.

title: Write unit and integration tests for soft-delete tombstones
description:
Comprehensive test suite for soft-delete tombstones in FSVI (bd-sot).

TEST MATRIX:

Unit Tests:
1. soft_delete_marks_record: soft_delete(doc_id) sets tombstone flag, is_deleted() returns true.
2. soft_delete_nonexistent: soft_delete for unknown doc_id returns Ok(false).
3. deleted_excluded_from_search: Tombstoned records not returned by top_k_search.
4. tombstone_count_accuracy: tombstone_count() matches number of soft_delete calls.
5. tombstone_ratio_calculation: tombstone_ratio() = tombstones / total_records.
6. needs_vacuum_threshold: needs_vacuum() returns true when ratio > 0.2 (default threshold).
7. vacuum_removes_tombstones: After vacuum(), tombstone_count() == 0, non-deleted records preserved.
8. vacuum_search_results_unchanged: Search results identical before and after vacuum (for non-deleted docs).
9. batch_delete: soft_delete_batch returns correct count of actually-deleted docs.
10. double_delete: soft_delete same doc twice — second call returns Ok(false), tombstone_count still 1.
11. flags_field_other_bits: Tombstone uses only bit 0; other bits in flags field remain untouched.

title: CRITICAL: search can return results in ALPHABETICAL doc_id order and report it as a successful Refined search (blend clamp collapse + missing quality-index guard)
description:
Found by user-directed semantic-path review (MossyPine, 2026-07-31); both halves personally re-verified at origin/main. This is the most user-visible defect found in either sweep. TWO defects that compound into one failure.

HALF A (blend.rs:73-85 NormBounds::apply): the function ends with blended.clamp(0.0, 1.0) where blended = t*norm + (1-t)*score and t = ((range-0.01)/0.04).clamp(0,1). When the score spread is narrow (range <= 0.05 so t < 1) the RAW score dominates the mix — and if raw scores sit OUTSIDE [0,1] the clamp flattens every one of them to exactly 0.0 (all-negative) or 1.0 (all >= 1). Worked example: fast scores in [-0.90,-0.88] => range 0.02, t 0.25, blended in [-0.675,-0.425] => ALL clamp to 0.0. All three sort comparators are score.total_cmp(..).then_with(|| left.doc_id.cmp(&right.doc_id)) (blend.rs:186-190, 281-285, 333-337), so with every score equal the ranking becomes ascending doc_id — ALPHABETICAL. Root cause: apply assumes cosine-in-[0,1] and uses clamp as a range guard, but is fed raw index scores that can be negative (true cosine) or unbounded (inner product). Internal inconsistency too: t gates on range > 0.01 while norm gates on range > f32::EPSILON.

HALF B (searcher.rs:2352-2354 should_run_quality): '!fast_only && quality_embedder.is_some()' asks whether a quality EMBEDDER is configured, never whether the INDEX has a quality tier. TwoTierIndex::has_quality_index() exists (index/two_tier.rs:1124) and the SYNC sibling calls it correctly (sync_searcher.rs:538-549, returning skip_reason quality_index_unavailable). With no quality tier the async path embeds the query, gets all-None quality scores, sets phase2_vectors_searched = 0, blends fast-only, and emits SearchPhase::Refined anyway.

COMPOUND FAILURE: with a quality-less index, Half B lets Phase 2 proceed; quality_scores are all None so the blend reduces to fast_bounds.apply(fast_score) with NO quality term to re-spread the distribution; if those fast scores are outside [0,1] with narrow spread, Half A flattens them and the doc_id tiebreak takes over. Net: SearchPhase::Refined is emitted, search_collect returns it in preference to the correctly-ordered Initial list (last-phase-wins, searcher.rs:1245), and its ordering is ALPHABETICAL BY DOC_ID. Every observability surface reports a successful two-phase refined search. Reachable in a common mid-migration state (quality embedder configured, index rebuilt fast-tier-only) and on any inner-product index.

FIX A: normalize before clamping — when range > f32::EPSILON use norm unconditionally (drop the t blend of the RAW score), or shift-and-scale the raw arm into [0,1] before the clamp. Add fixtures with all-negative and all->1 score sets asserting output order is NOT doc_id-ascending.
FIX B: should_run_quality gains '&& self.index.has_quality_index()' and skip_reason gains quality_index_unavailable, matching the sync sibling.
close_reason: Fixed both compound failure paths: all finite non-degenerate blend scores now normalize before clamping, preserving narrow negative and >1 rankings across all three blend implementations; async quality refinement now requires a real quality index and reports quality_index_unavailable without invoking the quality embedder. Strict-remote focused regressions, full fusion all-features tests, workspace check, and workspace clippy -D warnings pass.

title: MRL Adaptive Dimensionality at Search Time
description:
Implement Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) adaptive dimensionality for search-time dimension truncation. MRL-trained models (which includes potion-128M and many modern sentence transformers) produce embeddings where the first N dimensions carry the most information. We can search with truncated embeddings for speed, then use full dimensions for re-scoring.

## Design

```rust
pub struct MrlConfig {
    pub search_dims: usize,     // Dimensions for initial scan (default: 64)
    pub rescore_dims: usize,    // Dimensions for re-scoring top candidates (default: full)
    pub rescore_top_k: usize,   // Re-score this many candidates (default: 3x limit)
    pub enabled: bool,          // Default: false
}

impl VectorIndex {
    /// Search using only first `search_dims` dimensions, then re-score top candidates
    /// with full `rescore_dims` dimensions for better accuracy.
    pub fn mrl_search(
        &self,
        query: &[f32],
        limit: usize,
        config: &MrlConfig,
    ) -> Vec<VectorHit>;
}
```

## Algorithm

1. Truncate query to first search_dims dimensions
2. Scan all vectors using only first search_dims dimensions (fewer multiply-accumulate ops)
3. Collect top rescore_top_k candidates
4. Re-score candidates using full rescore_dims dimensions
5. Return top limit results

## Performance Model

- Standard search (384 dims): 384 multiply-accumulate per vector
- MRL search (64 + rescore 30): 64*N + 384*30 = 64N + 11520
- Break-even at N ≈ 36 vectors. For N > 100, MRL is faster.
- For 10K vectors: 640K vs 3.84M ops = 6x speedup on initial scan
- Net speedup depends on rescore_top_k but typically 2-4x for large indices

## SIMD Considerations

- 64 dims = 8 f32x8 operations (perfect alignment)
- 128 dims = 16 f32x8 operations
- Truncation points should be multiples of 8 for SIMD efficiency

## Index Format

No FSVI changes needed. We store full-dimension vectors and truncate at search time. The dimension information is in the header, and truncation is a runtime operation.

## Why This Matters

For large indices (100K+ vectors), search latency is dominated by the dot product scan. MRL gives a 2-4x speedup with minimal quality loss because the first 64 dimensions of MRL-trained models capture 90%+ of the variance. This is particularly valuable for the fast tier where latency budget is tight (<15ms).

## Testing

- Unit: truncated search returns same top-1 as full search (on MRL-trained embeddings)
- Unit: search_dims must be <= actual dimension
- Unit: SIMD alignment (search_dims multiple of 8)
- Unit: rescore_top_k < limit → fall back to full search
- Integration: MRL search quality vs full search (recall@10 comparison)
- Benchmark: speedup factor for various index sizes and search_dims

title: Index Warm-Up and Adaptive Prefault Strategy
description:
Implement index warm-up and adaptive page prefaulting for memory-mapped FSVI indices. Cold-start latency for mmap'd indices can be 10-100x higher than warm due to page faults. This bead adds controlled prefaulting to eliminate cold-start variance.

## Background

Frankensearch's FSVI indices are memory-mapped for zero-copy access. This is optimal for steady-state performance: the OS page cache keeps frequently-accessed pages in memory, and search reads directly from mapped memory without any copying. However, the first search after process start (or after memory pressure evicts pages) triggers a cascade of page faults that makes cold-start search dramatically slower.

For xf with 50K documents (~20MB index), cold search is approximately 50ms vs ~1ms warm — a 50x difference. For larger indices, this gap grows. This latency variance is problematic for interactive applications where consistent sub-10ms response times are expected.

## Design

### Configuration

```rust
pub struct WarmUpConfig {
    pub strategy: WarmUpStrategy,
    pub max_bytes: usize,        // Budget: don't prefault more than this (default: 256MB)
    pub parallel_readers: usize, // Concurrent prefault threads (default: 2)
}

pub enum WarmUpStrategy {
    None,                        // No prefaulting (current behavior)
    Full,                        // Touch every page sequentially
    Header,                      // Prefault header + record table only (smallest footprint)
    Adaptive(AdaptiveConfig),    // Heat-map based intelligent prefaulting
}

pub struct AdaptiveConfig {
    pub heat_decay: f64,         // Exponential decay factor (default: 0.95)
    pub min_heat: f64,           // Minimum heat to prefault (default: 0.1)
}
```

### Adaptive Strategy

The adaptive strategy learns which pages are actually accessed during typical queries:

1. Maintain a per-page heat map: 1 bit per 4KB page = 32KB overhead for a 1GB index
2. Increment heat on every page access (detected via access pattern tracking at the VectorIndex level)
3. Heat decays exponentially per search cycle: heat *= heat_decay
4. On warm-up, prefault pages above min_heat threshold in heat-descending order (hottest pages first)
5. Stop when max_bytes budget is exhausted

This means after a few search cycles, the system learns that (for example) the header, record table, and the first 30% of vector slabs are "hot" and should be prefaulted, while the remaining 70% of vectors (rarely-accessed tail) can be faulted on demand.

### OS Integration

- Linux: `madvise(MADV_WILLNEED)` to request kernel prefaulting
- macOS: `madvise(MADV_WILLNEED)` (same API, different kernel behavior)
- Fallback: sequential read through targeted pages for portability on other platforms

## Justification

In production, frankensearch indices are memory-mapped for zero-copy access. But the first search after process start (or after memory pressure evicts pages) is dramatically slower due to page faults. Prefaulting eliminates this variance.

The adaptive strategy is key: rather than always prefaulting the entire index (wasteful for large indices where only a fraction of pages are typically accessed), we learn which pages are actually accessed during typical queries and only prefault those. This provides the benefits of full prefaulting (consistent latency) with a fraction of the memory and I/O cost.

## Considerations

- Memory pressure: prefaulting competes with other processes for page cache space. The max_bytes budget prevents frankensearch from evicting other processes' pages.
- Background prefaulting: warm-up should run in background threads so it doesn't block the first search. If a search arrives before warm-up completes, it proceeds normally (with possible page faults for non-prefaulted pages).
- Multiple indices: when multiple FSVI indices are open (e.g., fast + quality embeddings), warm-up should respect the total max_bytes budget across all indices.
- Interaction with S3-FIFO cache (bd-l7v): the cache and prefaulting are complementary — cache handles repeated access patterns, prefaulting handles cold start.

## Testing

- [ ] Unit: WarmUpStrategy::None is a no-op (no system calls)
- [ ] Unit: WarmUpStrategy::Header only touches header + record table bytes
- [ ] Unit: heat map increment/decay math is correct
- [ ] Unit: max_bytes budget is respected (never prefault more than budget)
- [ ] Unit: heat map size calculation for various index sizes
- [ ] Integration: verify cold-start latency improvement (before/after warm-up, measure p50/p99)
- [ ] Integration: verify warm-up completes within reasonable time (< 2s for 256MB budget)
- [ ] Benchmark: prefault overhead vs cold search latency savings (quantify the tradeoff)

title: Implement robust statistics primitives for search monitoring
description:
Implement robust statistics primitives for search monitoring that are stable under outliers and heavy-tailed latency distributions. Replace mean/stddev with Median+MAD, Huber M-estimator, and streaming t-digest for zero-allocation quantile estimation.

Graveyard entry: §12.15 Robust Statistics Primitives + §9.4 Sketching & Streaming
EV score: 48 (Impact=3, Confidence=4, Reuse=4, Effort=1, Friction=1)
Priority tier: A

Architecture:
pub struct RobustMetrics {
    tdigest: TDigest,           // Streaming quantiles (any percentile)
    median_mad: MedianMAD,      // Robust center + spread
    huber: HuberEstimator,      // Outlier-resistant mean
    count: u64,
    last_reset: Instant,
}

Components:

1. TDigest (streaming quantile estimation):
   - Compression parameter: 100 (default)
   - Memory: ~4KB per metric stream
   - Update: O(log delta) per observation
   - Query: any quantile in O(delta) — p50, p90, p95, p99, p999
   - Merge: two t-digests can be merged (for per-thread → global aggregation)
   - Use existing `tdigest` crate (or implement ~200 lines)

2. Median + MAD (Median Absolute Deviation):
   - Robust center: median (breakdown point 50%)
   - Robust spread: MAD = median(|x_i - median|) * 1.4826
   - Requires sorted window; use circular buffer of last N observations (N=1000)

3. Huber M-estimator:
   - Iteratively reweighted least squares with tuning constant k=1.345
   - Breakdown point: min(k, 1-k) ≈ 20%
   - For normally-distributed data, converges to mean (no regression)
   - Streaming variant: exponentially weighted Huber mean

4. HyperLogLog (cardinality estimation):
   - Estimate unique queries, unique doc_ids in results
   - Memory: 12KB for <2% error
   - Use existing `hyperloglog` crate

Integration into TwoTierMetrics (bd-3un.24):
- Replace raw latency fields with RobustMetrics
- TwoTierMetrics.fast_latency → RobustMetrics (t-digest p50/p90/p99)
- TwoTierMetrics.refine_latency → RobustMetrics
- TwoTierMetrics.query_count → HyperLogLog (unique queries)

Concurrency: Per-thread RobustMetrics with periodic merge (lock-free via atomic swap of TDigest).

Budgeted mode: <500ns per metric update. Memory: ~4KB per metric × ~6 metrics = ~24KB total.

Fallback: Raw metric recording (f64 values) — zero impact on search correctness.

File: frankensearch-core/src/metrics.rs

Reference: Dunning & Ertl (2019) "t-digest", Huber (1981) "Robust Statistics", Flajolet et al. (2007) "HyperLogLog"
Baseline comparator: mean/stddev (current), P2 quantile estimator (bd-3un.24 comment — t-digest is more flexible: any quantile, not just predetermined)

Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
REVIEW FIX — Mathematical corrections and performance reconciliation:

1. HUBER BREAKDOWN POINT CORRECTION: The body states "Breakdown point: min(k, 1-k) ≈ 20%". This is INCORRECT. The Huber M-estimator of location has a breakdown point of 1/(n+1) → 0% as n→∞. It has a bounded influence function (which is different from breakdown point). The 1.345 tuning constant gives 95% asymptotic efficiency under normality.

   CORRECTED TEXT: "The Huber M-estimator with k=1.345 has a bounded influence function (robust to individual outliers) and 95% asymptotic efficiency under normality. Breakdown point is 0% (like all M-estimators of location without scale). For true breakdown robustness, pair with MAD scale estimate."

   For this use case (latency monitoring with occasional outliers), bounded influence is sufficient — we don't expect 50% of observations to be corrupted.

2. MEDIANMAD PERFORMANCE RECONCILIATION: Computing exact median on a circular buffer of N=1000 requires O(N log N) sorting or O(N) quickselect — both exceed the "<500ns per update" budget.

   FIX: Use the t-digest (already in RobustMetrics) for median estimation instead of maintaining a separate sorted window. T-digest p50 is accurate to within ~0.5% and update is O(log delta) ≈ O(1) amortized.

   REVISED MedianMAD:
   pub struct MedianMAD {
       tdigest: TDigest,  // REUSE the same t-digest for median
       // MAD = median(|x_i - median|) — also computed via a second t-digest
       deviation_tdigest: TDigest,
   }

   This eliminates the separate circular buffer and meets the <500ns budget.

3. HYPERLOGLOG PRECISION: Add "precision parameter p=14 (16,384 registers, ~12KB, standard error 0.81%)" to the body.

4. TEST REQUIREMENT ADDITIONS:
   - Huber: verify bounded influence (inserting one extreme outlier shifts estimate by < 1 MAD)
   - MedianMAD via t-digest: p50 within 1% of true median on 10K normal samples
   - MedianMAD: MAD within 2% of true MAD on 10K normal samples
   - Performance: 10K metric updates complete in < 5ms total (< 500ns amortized)

title: Quality-Tier Circuit Breaker
description:
Implement a circuit breaker pattern for the quality tier (Phase 2) of the TwoTierSearcher. When the quality tier is consistently slow, failing, or not improving results, the circuit breaker trips and subsequent queries skip Phase 2 entirely, returning only Phase 1 (fast) results until the circuit resets.

This is a simpler, more pragmatic alternative to the full sequential testing gate (bd-2ps). While bd-2ps uses e-processes for statistically rigorous decisions, this circuit breaker uses simple health metrics for operational reliability.

## Design

```rust
pub struct CircuitBreakerConfig {
    pub enabled: bool,                    // Default: true
    pub failure_threshold: u32,           // Consecutive failures to trip (default: 5)
    pub latency_threshold_ms: u64,        // Quality tier latency to count as "slow" (default: 500ms)
    pub improvement_threshold: f64,       // Min Kendall tau improvement to count as "useful" (default: 0.05)
    pub half_open_interval_ms: u64,       // Try quality tier again after this (default: 30000ms)
    pub reset_threshold: u32,             // Consecutive successes in half-open to close (default: 3)
}

pub enum CircuitState {
    Closed,     // Normal: quality tier active
    Open,       // Tripped: skip quality tier
    HalfOpen,   // Testing: try quality tier on next query
}

pub struct CircuitBreaker {
    state: AtomicU8,
    consecutive_failures: AtomicU32,
    consecutive_successes: AtomicU32,
    last_trip_time: AtomicU64,
    metrics: CircuitMetrics,
}

pub struct CircuitMetrics {
    pub trips: u64,
    pub resets: u64,
    pub queries_skipped: u64,
    pub avg_skip_savings_ms: f64,
}
```

## Failure Conditions (any one triggers a failure count)

1. Quality tier exceeds latency_threshold_ms
2. Quality tier returns an error
3. Quality tier results have Kendall tau < improvement_threshold vs fast results (not improving ranking)

## State Machine

- **Closed → Open**: after failure_threshold consecutive failures
- **Open → HalfOpen**: after half_open_interval_ms
- **HalfOpen → Closed**: after reset_threshold consecutive successes
- **HalfOpen → Open**: on any failure

## Why This Matters

The quality tier (MiniLM-L6-v2 at ~128ms) is the largest latency contributor. In some scenarios — system under load, model warm-up, or queries where fast-tier results are already excellent — the quality tier adds latency without improving results. The circuit breaker automatically adapts, giving consumers consistently fast responses when quality refinement isn't helping.

This pairs with bd-1cr (robust statistics) for computing rolling latency percentiles and with the existing TwoTierMetrics for Kendall tau calculation.

## Testing

- Unit: circuit starts Closed
- Unit: consecutive failures trip to Open
- Unit: timeout transitions to HalfOpen
- Unit: successes in HalfOpen reset to Closed
- Unit: failure in HalfOpen returns to Open
- Unit: metrics tracking (trips, resets, queries_skipped)
- Integration: circuit breaker with simulated slow quality tier
- Integration: verify no quality tier calls when Open
- Benchmark: circuit breaker overhead (should be <1μs per query)

title: Incremental Append-Only FSVI Index Updates
description:
Implement WAL-based append-only mutation for the FSVI vector index format. Currently, any document addition requires a full index rebuild. This is the #1 usability friction point for frankensearch consumers.

## Background

The FSVI (FrankenSearch Vector Index) format is frankensearch's custom binary vector index. It stores document embeddings in a compact, memory-mappable layout optimized for top-k cosine similarity search. However, the current design is fully immutable: adding a single document requires reading the entire index, appending the new record in memory, and writing a completely new index file. For large indices (e.g., xf with 50K+ tweets), this means re-processing the entire corpus on every addition.

## Design

### Append Buffer (WAL)
New vectors are appended to a separate `.fsvi.wal` file. This file uses the same binary layout as the main index (raw records + vector slabs) but without the header. This keeps the WAL format trivially compatible with the main index reader.

### Search Merges
`top_k_search` reads both the main index and the WAL, merges results via a unified BinaryHeap. The WAL is small relative to the main index, so the merge overhead is minimal.

### Compaction
When the WAL exceeds a configurable threshold (default: 10% of main index size or 1000 records), compact by rewriting main index + WAL into a new main index. This is a background operation that does not block reads.

### Atomic Swap
Compaction writes to `.fsvi.new`, then `rename()` over the old file (atomic on POSIX). This ensures readers never see a partially-written index.

### fsync Discipline
WAL append is fsync'd per batch (not per record) for durability without excessive I/O. Single appends are batches of size 1.

## API Surface

```rust
impl VectorIndex {
    pub fn append(&mut self, doc_id: &str, vector: &[f32]) -> Result<(), SearchError>;
    pub fn append_batch(&mut self, entries: &[(String, Vec<f32>)]) -> Result<(), SearchError>;
    pub fn compact(&mut self) -> Result<CompactionStats, SearchError>;
    pub fn needs_compaction(&self) -> bool;
    pub fn wal_record_count(&self) -> usize;
}
```

## Performance Targets

- Single append: <100us (excluding fsync)
- Batch append (100 docs): <5ms
- Search overhead from WAL merge: <10% vs main-only search (for WAL size < 10% of main)

## Justification

Without incremental append, every consumer must rebuild the entire index when adding a single document. For xf (50K+ tweets), this means re-embedding everything. Append-only makes frankensearch practical for live, growing datasets. This is the single highest-impact usability improvement for all three consumers (cass, xf, mcp_agent_mail_rust).

## Considerations

- WAL file must be crash-safe: partial writes should be detectable (length check + CRC per batch)
- Compaction must not block concurrent reads
- Memory-mapped WAL: for small WALs, mmap is fine; for large WALs approaching compaction threshold, sequential read may be preferred
- Interaction with soft-delete tombstones: WAL entries can also be tombstoned, and compaction naturally removes them

## Testing

- [ ] Unit: append single vector, verify searchable immediately
- [ ] Unit: append batch, verify all vectors searchable
- [ ] Unit: compaction reduces file count, search results unchanged
- [ ] Unit: WAL threshold detection (needs_compaction)
- [ ] Unit: wal_record_count accuracy
- [ ] Integration: concurrent append + search (verify no corruption)
- [ ] Integration: crash recovery (partial WAL write detection)
- [ ] Benchmark: append latency (single and batch)
- [ ] Benchmark: search overhead vs WAL size (1%, 5%, 10%)
acceptance_criteria:
1. The feature is fully implemented according to this bead design, scope, and referenced files or modules.
2. Integration with dependent components is complete and behavior remains correct across normal and degraded flows.
3. Edge and error cases are explicitly handled with deterministic outcomes and clear reason codes or errors.
4. Unit and integration tests (and e2e where relevant) are added, passing, and include detailed structured logging assertions.
5. Performance and resource expectations in the bead are validated and documented with reproducible evidence.
6. Every explicit checklist item in the bead description is implemented and verified by automated tests or validation commands.

comments.text: REFINEMENT PASS 1: Added cross-dep on bd-sot (soft-delete tombstones). Compaction MUST be tombstone-aware: when rewriting main index + WAL into new main index, tombstoned entries in both WAL and main index must be dropped. This unifies vacuum (bd-sot) and compaction (bd-1hw) into a single operation. Also: WAL append does NOT need asupersync -- it is a synchronous file I/O operation (write + optional fsync). The background compaction thread could use Rayon or a plain std::thread since it is CPU+IO bound, not async IO. If the index refresh worker (bd-3un.28) uses asupersync, then compaction scheduling should integrate with that workers Cx lifecycle.

Compaction can be implemented without tombstone awareness in the first pass -- it simply merges WAL records into the main index. Tombstone-aware compaction (dropping deleted records during merge) is a SOFT interaction that should be added when bd-sot is implemented. When bd-sot lands, compaction should be updated to skip tombstoned records during the merge pass. This avoids a priority inversion (P1 blocked by P2).

title: Use frankenjax vmap semantics for automatic batch embedding vectorization
description:
When frankenjax matures, use its vmap (vectorized map) transform to automatically lift single-document embedding functions into optimally batched versions, eliminating manual batch-size tuning and improving indexing throughput.

PROBLEM STATEMENT:
frankensearch's Embedder trait defines embed(&Cx, &str) -> Vec<f32> for single documents. For bulk indexing (10K+ documents), calling embed() in a loop wastes ~95% of ML model inference overhead because ONNX/transformer setup cost is nearly fixed regardless of batch size. The current solution is manual batching (bd-i37 BatchCoalescer), which requires hand-tuning max_batch_size, max_wait_ms, and priority lanes.

WHAT VMAP PROVIDES:
frankenjax's vmap transform takes a function f: T -> U and produces f_batched: [T] -> [U] that:
1. Automatically infers optimal batch dimensions from the input
2. Manages memory layout for cache-efficient batch processing
3. Composes with other transforms (jit for fusion, grad if needed)
4. Handles remainders (last batch < batch_size) transparently

RELATIONSHIP TO bd-i37 (BATCH COALESCING) — COMPLEMENTARY, NOT REPLACEMENT:
- bd-i37 handles the CONCURRENCY problem: coalescing multiple concurrent callers' embed() requests into shared batches with deadline scheduling and priority lanes
- bd-1pfc handles the COMPUTATION problem: making the underlying model inference itself batch-efficient
- They compose: BatchCoalescer collects requests -> vmap-lifted embed processes them as an optimal batch
- Without frankenjax: BatchCoalescer calls embed() in a loop or uses a manually implemented embed_batch()
- With frankenjax: BatchCoalescer calls vmap(embed)(batch) which automatically optimizes the forward pass

CONCRETE INTEGRATION:
1. Extend BatchEmbedder extension trait (from bd-i37):
   - Auto-derive embed_batch via vmap: embed_batch = frankenjax::vmap(embed)
   - The vmap-lifted version handles padding, batching, and memory layout
   - Embedder impls that don't manually implement BatchEmbedder get it for free via vmap

2. Index building pipeline (frankensearch-index or frankensearch-embed):
   - Replace sequential for doc in docs { embed(doc) } with:
     let embed_batch = frankenjax::vmap(|doc| embedder.embed(cx, doc));
     let all_embeddings = embed_batch(documents);
   - frankenjax handles chunking into optimal batch sizes internally

3. Compose with jit (optional, future stretch goal):
   - frankenjax::jit(frankenjax::vmap(embed)) would fuse the batch operation
   - Depends on frankenjax jit maturity for transformer architectures

EXPECTED THROUGHPUT IMPROVEMENT:
- Current (sequential embed): 128ms/doc with MiniLM -> 1280s for 10K docs
- With manual batching (bd-i37, batch_size=32): ~140ms/32 docs -> ~44s for 10K docs (29x)
- With vmap (auto-optimal batching): comparable to manual but with zero tuning and better memory layout
- The win is NOT faster than manual batching — it's SIMPLER (no batch_size parameter) and COMPOSABLE (works with any embedder automatically)

FEATURE FLAG:
`vmap = ['dep:frankenjax']` in frankensearch-embed/Cargo.toml
- Off by default
- When enabled, BatchEmbedder gets a default vmap-based implementation
- When disabled, BatchEmbedder falls back to sequential embed() loop
- The `full` meta-feature should include it when frankenjax is mature

CRATE PLACEMENT:
- frankensearch-embed/src/vmap_batch.rs: vmap-based BatchEmbedder blanket impl
- Update frankensearch-embed/src/auto_detect.rs: wire vmap into EmbedderStack when feature enabled

ERROR HANDLING AND FALLBACK:
- If frankenjax::vmap panics or returns error on a batch: fall back to sequential embed() per doc
- Log WARN on first fallback with error context, suppress subsequent for 60s
- Never let vmap failure block indexing or search — vmap is an optimization, not a correctness requirement
- If vmap produces output of wrong dimension: reject entire batch, fall back to sequential, log ERROR

DEPENDENCY CHAIN:
- Hard dependency: bd-3un.3 (Embedder trait must exist)
- Soft dependency: bd-i37 (BatchCoalescer provides the concurrency layer that calls embed_batch)
- Soft dependency: bd-2ba5 (frankentorch) since vmap over frankentorch inference is the ideal composition — vmap over ONNX via fastembed may not work (ONNX Runtime has its own batching)
acceptance_criteria:
1. vmap-lifted embed produces identical embeddings to sequential embed (cosine similarity > 0.9999 per vector)
2. vmap-lifted embed_batch handles non-divisible batch sizes correctly (e.g., 10007 docs with implicit batch_size=32)
3. Indexing throughput with vmap >= throughput with manual batching (no regression)
4. Memory usage during batch indexing is bounded (peak RSS < 2x sequential for same corpus)
5. vmap composes correctly with BatchCoalescer (bd-i37) for concurrent search queries
6. All existing Embedder tests pass when embed_batch is auto-derived via vmap
7. Works with all three embedder backends: hash, model2vec, fastembed/frankentorch
8. Fallback to sequential works when vmap errors (no search/indexing failure)
9. Feature flag compiles correctly: with vmap, without vmap, with vmap+fastembed, with vmap+frankentorch
notes: Deferred by backlog harmonization pass. Re-entry criteria: (1) Sprint-1 keystone program bd-1zxn closed, (2) release gate bd-ehuk closed, (3) proof-lane contract bd-bobf has at least one completed exemplar, and (4) concrete EV score >= 2.0 with measured hotspot evidence.

title: Fix rrf_fuse_reference_full_sort double-counting within-source duplicates

title: Write unit and integration tests for embedding batch coalescing
description:
Comprehensive test suite for embedding batch coalescing with deadline scheduling (bd-i37).

TEST MATRIX:

Unit Tests:
1. single_request_dispatched: Submit 1 request, verify dispatched within max_wait_ms.
2. full_batch_immediate: Submit max_batch_size requests, verify dispatched immediately (no waiting).
3. interactive_priority_early_dispatch: Interactive request in batch triggers early dispatch (doesn't wait for full batch).
4. deadline_enforcement: Request with tight deadline dispatched before max_wait_ms.
5. background_accumulation: Background-priority requests accumulate until max_batch_size or max_wait_ms.
6. mixed_priority_scheduling: Interactive + background requests batched together, interactive sets batch deadline.
7. correct_result_routing: 10 concurrent callers, each receives their OWN embedding (not another caller's).
8. batch_embedder_fallback: When embedder doesn't support batch, fall back to sequential.
9. empty_text_handling: Empty string request handled gracefully.
10. max_batch_size_respected: Never dispatch a batch larger than max_batch_size.

Integration Tests:
11. throughput_improvement: Measure throughput with batching vs without (expect 5-30x for ONNX models).
12. concurrent_interactive_and_background: Mix of search queries (interactive) and index-building (background), verify search latency not impacted.
13. graceful_shutdown: Shutdown coalescer, verify all pending requests receive results or error.

Benchmarks:
14. bench_coalescer_overhead: Per-request overhead of coalescing machinery (target: <10us).
15. bench_throughput_scaling: Throughput vs batch size (1, 4, 8, 16, 32) with FNV-1a and Model2Vec embedders.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The requested test suite is implemented for the target feature or module and wired into normal test commands and CI lanes.
2. Tests cover happy paths, edge and boundary conditions, and failure or degraded scenarios, including concurrency and cancellation where applicable.
3. Tests assert structured logs, metrics, or reason codes so failures are diagnosable without manual reproduction.
4. Test execution is deterministic and reproducible and emits actionable artifacts on failure (fixtures, traces, summaries, replay context).
5. Documented coverage and pass criteria are met, and no flaky behavior is introduced.
close_reason: done

title: Add profile variant comparison to search quality harness
Implement adaptive fusion parameters via Bayesian online learning
description:
Implement adaptive fusion parameters with Bayesian online learning so rank fusion behavior improves from observed usage while staying auditable and safe.

## Background
Hybrid ranking currently uses fixed constants (RRF K and fast/quality blend factor). Fixed knobs are simple but cannot adapt to query mix or real feedback.

## Design
- Blend adaptation: Beta-Bernoulli posterior per query class (`QueryClass`) from implicit relevance signals (click/skip/select/dwell).
- RRF-K adaptation: Normal-Normal posterior (location parameter), replacing the incorrect Gamma-Normal framing.
- Optional Thompson sampling for controlled exploration with deterministic seed hooks for tests.
- Per-class + global fallback posteriors; minimum sample gates before adaptation.
- Safety clamps and hysteresis to prevent parameter thrash.
- Structured evidence events emitted per update (query class, prior/posterior params, chosen K/blend, signal source).

## Integration
- Consumes signal stream from feedback pathways (e.g., bd-2tv when enabled).
- Exposes chosen parameters to `TwoTierSearcher`/fusion path and to observability contracts.
- No tokio; runtime interactions follow asupersync usage in surrounding pipeline.

## Testing Focus
- Posterior math correctness and numerical stability.
- Convergence and boundedness under synthetic streams.
- Per-query-class isolation and fallback correctness.
- Artifact-rich integration runs proving relevance uplift is measured, not assumed.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Bayesian updater is implemented with Beta-Bernoulli for blend and Normal-Normal for RRF-K, with deterministic clamps and no NaN/inf propagation.
2) Per-query-class posteriors are maintained with global fallback; adaptation remains disabled until configurable minimum sample thresholds are met.
3) Unit tests cover prior recovery, posterior convergence, sampling bounds, class isolation, and malformed-signal handling.
4) Integration tests run adaptive fusion through the end-to-end search pipeline and emit structured evidence logs tied to query/session IDs.
5) E2E scripts produce replayable artifacts (config snapshot, signal trace, posterior timeline, ranking deltas) suitable for regression diagnostics.
close_reason: Fully implemented: AdaptiveFusion with Beta-Bernoulli blend and Normal-Normal K posteriors in frankensearch-fusion/src/adaptive.rs (691 lines, 22 tests)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
Implement Bayesian online learning for adaptive fusion parameters (RRF K constant and blend factor). Instead of fixed constants, maintain conjugate priors that update from implicit relevance feedback.

MATHEMATICAL FOUNDATION:

1. Adaptive Blend Factor via Beta-Bernoulli Model:
   - Prior: Beta(7, 3) encoding the initial 0.7 blend factor
   - Update: observe whether quality-tier reranking improved results (via click/dwell signals)
   - Posterior: Beta(7 + successes, 3 + failures)
   - Blend factor = E[posterior] = alpha / (alpha + beta)
   - Thompson sampling variant: sample blend factor from posterior for exploration

2. Adaptive RRF K via Gamma-Normal Model:
   - Prior: Gamma(60, 1) encoding the K=60 default
   - Update: observe fusion quality (Kemeny distance between fused ranking and click-derived ranking)
   - Posterior update via conjugate machinery
   - K = E[posterior]

3. Per-Query-Class Adaptation:
   - Maintain separate Beta posteriors per query classification (from bd-3un.43):
     Short keyword queries may prefer higher K (uniform weighting)
     Natural language queries may prefer lower K (top-heavy weighting)
     Identifier queries may prefer blend_factor closer to 0.0 (fast tier is fine)

4. Evidence Ledger:
   - Every search emits a structured record:
     query_hash, query_class, blend_factor_used, k_used, fast_ndcg, quality_ndcg, blended_ndcg, rank_correlation
   - Enables offline analysis and posterior initialization for new deployments

5. Regret Bound:
   - Under Beta-Bernoulli Thompson sampling: E[Regret(T)] is O(sqrt(T log T))
   - Provably converges to optimal parameters

Implementation:

pub struct AdaptiveFusionParams {
    blend_alpha: AtomicF64,   // Beta posterior for blend factor
    blend_beta: AtomicF64,
    k_alpha: AtomicF64,       // Gamma posterior for RRF K
    k_beta: AtomicF64,
    min_samples: usize,       // Don't adapt until N queries (default: 50)
}

File: frankensearch-fusion/src/adaptive.rs

This is a pure addition. The fixed defaults remain as the zero-observation case. No API changes needed; TwoTierConfig gains an optional adaptive_params field.

Alien-artifact characteristics:
- Mathematical rigor: conjugate Bayesian posteriors with formal update rules
- Explainability: evidence ledger tracks every decision
- Formal guarantees: Thompson sampling regret bound
- Graceful degradation: falls back to fixed defaults with insufficient data
- Operational excellence: O(1) per query, two floats of state per parameter

title: Implement score calibration service (Platt/isotonic/temperature)
description:
Implement a ScoreCalibrator trait and calibration layer that converts heterogeneous raw model scores (BM25 [0,inf), cosine [-1,1], reranker logits (-inf,inf)) into calibrated probabilities [0,1] before fusion. This makes blend_factor and RRF score combination mathematically meaningful.

Graveyard entry: §12.16 Calibration Service Abstraction
EV score: 50 (Impact=5, Confidence=4, Reuse=5, Effort=2, Friction=1)
Priority tier: A

Architecture:
pub trait ScoreCalibrator: Send + Sync {
    fn calibrate(&self, raw_score: f64) -> f64;  // raw -> [0,1] probability
    fn calibrate_batch(&self, scores: &mut [f64]);
    fn ece(&self) -> f64;  // Expected Calibration Error
    fn name(&self) -> &str;
}

Implementations:
1. Identity — passthrough (default, backward-compatible)
2. TemperatureScaling — single parameter T: calibrated = sigmoid(score / T)
   - T learned offline via NLL minimization on validation set
   - O(1) per score, <10ns overhead
3. PlattScaling — logistic regression: calibrated = sigmoid(a * score + b)
   - Parameters (a, b) fit offline via L-BFGS on held-out data
   - O(1) per score
4. IsotonicRegression — non-parametric monotonic mapping
   - Learned offline: piecewise-constant monotone function
   - O(log n) per score (binary search on breakpoints)
   - Guaranteed monotonic (preserves ranking order within each source)

Integration points:
- Before RRF fusion (bd-3un.20): calibrate lexical + semantic scores
- Before two-tier blending (bd-3un.21): calibrate fast + quality scores
- After reranking (bd-3un.26): calibrate reranker output (replaces raw sigmoid)

Calibration training (offline):
- Use test fixture corpus (bd-3un.38) as calibration set
- For each score source: fit calibrator on (raw_score, relevance_label) pairs
- Store calibration parameters as JSON artifact (sha256 signed)
- Load at search time; recalibrate periodically

Monitoring:
- ECE (Expected Calibration Error): partition [0,1] into 10 bins, measure |avg_confidence - accuracy| per bin
- Brier score: mean squared error of calibrated probabilities vs relevance
- ECE > 0.10 for 5 windows → automatic fallback to Identity + trigger retrain

Budgeted mode: <1us per score calibration. Memory: ~1KB for isotonic breakpoints.

Isomorphism proof: Isotonic regression is monotonic by construction → calibrated scores preserve original ranking order within each source. Prove: for all i<j, raw[i] <= raw[j] implies calibrated[i] <= calibrated[j].

File: frankensearch-fusion/src/calibration.rs

Reference: Platt (1999) "Probabilistic outputs for SVMs", Zadrozny & Elkan (2002) "Transforming classifier scores", Guo et al. (2017) "On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks"
Baseline comparator: Raw score passthrough (current), naive min-max (bd-3un.19)

1. The feature is fully implemented according to this bead design, scope, and referenced files or modules.
2. Integration with dependent components is complete and behavior remains correct across normal and degraded flows.
3. Edge and error cases are explicitly handled with deterministic outcomes and clear reason codes or errors.
4. Unit and integration tests (and e2e where relevant) are added, passing, and include detailed structured logging assertions.
5. Performance and resource expectations in the bead are validated and documented with reproducible evidence.

comments.text:
REFINEMENT PASS 1 — Architecture clarifications and integration notes:

1. DEPENDENCY JUSTIFICATION: This bead depends on bd-3un.19 (normalization) because calibration REPLACES naive min-max normalization as the score preparation step. Once calibration is available, the fusion pipeline should prefer calibrated scores over normalized scores. The normalization module still exists as a simpler fallback and for contexts where calibration data isn't available.

2. RELATIONSHIP WITH bd-21g (Bayesian adaptive fusion): Calibrated scores make the Bayesian posterior updates in bd-21g more meaningful. When scores are properly calibrated to [0,1] probabilities, the Beta-Bernoulli blend factor updates have clearer semantics (success = calibrated quality score > calibrated fast score). This is a soft dependency — bd-21g works without calibration but works BETTER with it.

3. CALIBRATION TRAINING PIPELINE: The offline calibration training should be a standalone binary/script (lives in examples/ or tools/) that:
   a. Loads test fixture corpus (bd-3un.38)
   b. Runs each scorer (BM25, fast cosine, quality cosine, reranker) on all query-doc pairs
   c. Fits calibrators using known relevance labels
   d. Serializes calibration parameters to JSON
   e. Writes to data_dir/calibration/<scorer_id>.json
   The CalibrationLayer loads these at search time.

4. ONLINE TEMPERATURE SCALING: For production use without offline calibration data, TemperatureScaling can be fit online using a simple gradient descent on the last N queries (where N=100). This is the recommended default for new deployments.

5. TEST REQUIREMENTS (covered by bd-3un.31): Add tests for:
   - Identity calibrator preserves scores exactly
   - Temperature scaling with T=1.0 equals sigmoid
   - Platt scaling monotonicity (higher raw score = higher calibrated score)
   - Isotonic regression monotonicity guarantee
   - ECE computation correctness on known distribution
   - Batch calibration matches sequential calibration
   - Round-trip: serialize calibrator params to JSON and reload

2. TEMPERATURE SCALING SCOPE: Temperature scaling (calibrated = sigmoid(score / T)) is most appropriate for:
   - Reranker output (cross-encoder logits) — ideal use case
   - Cosine similarity scores (bounded [-1, 1]) — acceptable

   It is LESS appropriate for:
   - Raw BM25 scores (unbounded [0, ∞)) — normalize to [0, 1] first
   - RRF scores (small values ~0.01-0.03) — Platt scaling is better here

   Add a recommendation: use TemperatureScaling for reranker, PlattScaling for BM25/RRF, IsotonicRegression for any source when sufficient calibration data exists.

3. PER-QUERY-CLASS CALIBRATION NOTE: Different query classes (Identifier vs NaturalLanguage) produce different score distributions. For best calibration:
   - Fit separate calibrators per (source, query_class) pair
   - This is a soft dependency on bd-3un.43 (query classification)
   - For V1: single calibrator per source is sufficient
   - For V2: per-query-class calibration with Mondrian-style partitioning

title: Typed Filter Predicates
description:
Add typed filter predicates that consumers can apply at search time to narrow results without modifying the index. Currently, filtering must happen post-search (wasteful) or by building separate indices (complex).

## Background

All three consumer codebases (cass, xf, mcp_agent_mail_rust) need to filter search results by document type, date range, or custom predicates. Without built-in filter support, each consumer reimplements filtering post-hoc, which loses the performance benefits of early filtering. Post-filtering is particularly wasteful for selective filters: if only 5% of documents match, the search engine computes scores for 20x more documents than necessary.

## Design

### Filter Trait

```rust
pub trait SearchFilter: Send + Sync {
    fn matches(&self, doc_id: &str, metadata: Option<&serde_json::Value>) -> bool;
    fn name(&self) -> &str;
}
```

### Built-in Filters

```rust
pub struct DocTypeFilter(HashSet<String>);              // Match doc_type field
pub struct DateRangeFilter(Option<i64>, Option<i64>);   // created_at range (unix timestamps)
pub struct BitsetFilter(HashSet<u64>);                  // Pre-computed doc_id_hash set
pub struct PredicateFilter(Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool + Send + Sync>);  // Arbitrary closure

pub struct FilterChain {
    filters: Vec<Box<dyn SearchFilter>>,
    mode: FilterMode,  // All (AND) or Any (OR)
}

pub enum FilterMode {
    All,  // AND: all filters must match
    Any,  // OR: any filter matching is sufficient
}
```

### Integration

**Vector search (FSVI)**: Filters are applied DURING the top-k scan, not after. This is the key performance insight. When scanning vectors for top-k cosine similarity, we check the filter predicate for each candidate and skip non-matching records. This means if you want the top-10 results matching doc_type="tweet", we scan vectors and skip non-tweets, rather than fetching top-100 and filtering to tweets. This is critical for performance when the filter is highly selective (e.g., <10% of documents match).

**Lexical search (Tantivy)**: Filters translate directly to BooleanQuery clauses with MUST clauses. Tantivy handles these natively and efficiently via its query engine. DocTypeFilter becomes a TermQuery, DateRangeFilter becomes a RangeQuery.

**RRF fusion**: For cross-source filters that operate on fused results, apply after fusion. This handles cases where the filter depends on combined metadata from multiple sources.

## Justification

- **cass**: needs to filter by session_id, message_type (user vs assistant), date range
- **xf**: needs to filter by tweet_type (original, retweet, reply), author, date range
- **mcp_agent_mail_rust**: needs to filter by sender, recipient, read/unread status, TTL expiration

Without built-in filter support, each consumer reimplements filtering post-hoc, losing early-exit performance benefits and duplicating logic across codebases.

## Considerations

- Filter cost: SearchFilter::matches should be cheap (O(1) ideally). Expensive filters should use BitsetFilter with pre-computed sets.
- Metadata availability: vector search may not have metadata readily available. The doc_id-based path (matching on ID alone) is always available; metadata-based filtering requires the metadata to be stored alongside vectors or looked up from Tantivy.
- Filter selectivity estimation: for very selective filters (<1% match rate), consider early termination heuristics to avoid scanning the entire index.
- Interaction with WAL (Idea 1): filters must also apply to WAL records during merged search.

## Testing

- [ ] Unit: DocTypeFilter matches/rejects correctly
- [ ] Unit: DateRangeFilter with None boundaries (open-ended ranges)
- [ ] Unit: DateRangeFilter with both boundaries set
- [ ] Unit: BitsetFilter with known hash set
- [ ] Unit: FilterChain AND semantics (all must match)
- [ ] Unit: FilterChain OR semantics (any match suffices)
- [ ] Unit: PredicateFilter with arbitrary closure
- [ ] Unit: empty FilterChain matches everything
- [ ] Integration: filtered vector search returns only matching results
- [ ] Integration: filtered lexical search translates to correct Tantivy query
- [ ] Integration: cross-source filter applied after RRF fusion
- [ ] Benchmark: early-exit filter vs post-filter performance (measure with 5%, 50%, 95% selectivity)

5. Performance and resource expectations in the bead are validated and documented with reproducible evidence.
6. Every explicit checklist item in the bead description is implemented and verified by automated tests or validation commands.

comments.text: Cross-reference: bd-2n6 (Negative/Exclusion Query Syntax) defines negative terms and phrases that functionally behave like exclusion filters. Consider whether negative query syntax should be implemented AS a filter predicate (a NegativeTermFilter wrapping the parsed negative terms) rather than as a separate search-time mechanism. This would unify the exclusion surface: consumers could use either the query syntax ('-foo') or the programmatic API (SearchFilter::exclude('foo')) with identical semantics. However, there's a performance argument for keeping them separate: Tantivy can handle MUST_NOT clauses more efficiently than post-hoc filter predicates, and semantic exclusion via embedding penalty is fundamentally different from predicate filtering. Recommendation: keep separate implementations but ensure they compose correctly when both are active on the same query.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
DESIGN CLARIFICATION: Metadata availability during vector search.

The SearchFilter trait has matches(doc_id, metadata) but FSVI stores only doc_id (via hash + string table) and flags. It does NOT store arbitrary metadata. This means:

DURING VECTOR SEARCH (frankensearch-index):
- Filters that operate on doc_id alone work directly: BitsetFilter, PredicateFilter
- Filters that need metadata (DocTypeFilter, DateRangeFilter) require an external metadata lookup

METADATA LOOKUP OPTIONS:
1. Consumer provides a metadata_fn: Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> Option<serde_json::Value>> to the search call
2. After FrankenSQLite integration (bd-3w1), metadata can be looked up from the document table
3. For Tantivy-backed searches, stored fields provide metadata natively

RECOMMENDED PATTERN:
- Vector search uses a TWO-PHASE approach: 
  Phase 1: Apply doc_id-only filters (BitsetFilter, PredicateFilter) during scan — these are O(1) per record
  Phase 2: For metadata-requiring filters, collect candidate doc_ids from Phase 1, batch-lookup metadata, then filter
- This avoids per-record metadata lookup during the hot scan loop
- Tantivy search applies all filters natively (stored fields are available)

IMPORTANT: The SearchFilter.matches() signature should support the two-phase pattern:
  fn matches_id(&self, doc_id: &str) -> Option<bool>  // Some(true/false) if decidable from id alone, None if needs metadata
  fn matches_full(&self, doc_id: &str, metadata: &serde_json::Value) -> bool  // Full check with metadata

This lets the vector search engine skip metadata lookup for filters that can decide on doc_id alone.

title: Replace ONNX Runtime with frankentorch for native Rust embedding and reranking inference
description:
When frankentorch matures to support transformer forward-pass inference, replace the ort (ONNX Runtime C++ bridge) and fastembed dependencies with pure-Rust inference. This eliminates frankensearch's heaviest native dependency and makes the entire search stack compilable with `cargo build` alone — no C++ toolchain, no ONNX shared libraries, no platform-specific binaries.

CURRENT C/C++ DEPENDENCY CHAIN:
- fastembed -> ort -> onnxruntime (C++ shared lib, ~150MB)
- frankensearch-rerank -> ort -> onnxruntime
- These cause: slow builds, CI complexity, platform-specific failures, large binary size

WHAT FRANKENTORCH MUST SUPPORT (maturity gate):
1. Load safetensors model files (MiniLM-L6-v2 is ~22M params, cross-encoder is ~33M params)
2. Tokenization via the tokenizers crate (already used by frankensearch-embed for model2vec)
3. 6-layer transformer forward pass: embedding -> multi-head attention -> feed-forward -> pooling
4. 12-layer transformer forward pass for cross-encoder (query-document pair scoring)
5. Numerical accuracy: output vectors must match ONNX Runtime within cosine similarity > 0.999
6. Performance: inference latency within 2x of ONNX Runtime (acceptable tradeoff for pure Rust)

FEATURE FLAG STRATEGY (critical for migration):
- New feature flag: `frankentorch = ['dep:frankentorch']` in frankensearch-embed and frankensearch-rerank
- Existing `fastembed` and `rerank` feature flags remain unchanged
- When both `fastembed` and `frankentorch` are enabled, frankentorch takes priority in auto-detection
- EmbedderStack auto-detection order: frankentorch (if available) -> fastembed -> model2vec -> hash
- Runtime fallback: if frankentorch inference panics/errors, fall back to fastembed if available

IMPLEMENTATION PLAN:
1. New file: frankensearch-embed/src/frankentorch_embedder.rs
   - Implements Embedder trait (embed, dimension, is_semantic, category)
   - Loads MiniLM-L6-v2 from safetensors
   - Forward pass: tokenize -> embed -> mean pool -> L2 normalize
   - Model path: same auto-detection logic as fastembed (XDG cache dir)

2. New file: frankensearch-rerank/src/frankentorch_reranker.rs
   - Implements Reranker trait (rerank)
   - Loads cross-encoder model from safetensors
   - Forward pass: tokenize(query, doc) -> transformer -> classifier head -> sigmoid
   - Produces scores in [0, 1] matching current FlashRank output semantics

3. Update frankensearch-embed/src/auto_detect.rs:
   - Add FrankentorchEmbedder to detection chain
   - Prefer frankentorch when feature is enabled and model is available

4. Update frankensearch/Cargo.toml feature flags:
   - `frankentorch` feature in relevant crates
   - `full` feature includes frankentorch

MIGRATION PATH:
- Phase 1: Add frankentorch as ALTERNATIVE backend (behind feature flag), fastembed remains default
- Phase 2: Run parity tests (see below) until all pass
- Phase 3: Make frankentorch the default when `full` feature is enabled
- Phase 4: Deprecate fastembed feature flag (but don't remove — downstream may depend on it)

LOGGING:
- INFO on startup: which inference backend was selected and why
- DEBUG per inference: model={name} input_tokens={n} latency_ms={ms} backend={frankentorch|ort}
- WARN on fallback: frankentorch -> fastembed fallback with error context
acceptance_criteria:
1. FrankentorchEmbedder implements Embedder trait and passes all existing embed tests
2. FrankentorchReranker implements Reranker trait and passes all existing rerank tests
3. Cosine similarity between frankentorch and ONNX outputs > 0.999 on fixture corpus
4. nDCG@10 with frankentorch backend >= nDCG@10 with ONNX backend on ground truth queries (no ranking regression)
5. Inference latency within 2x of ONNX Runtime (measured on fixture corpus)
6. `cargo build --features frankentorch` succeeds with no C/C++ toolchain installed
7. Feature flag combinations compile: frankentorch alone, fastembed alone, both, neither
8. Auto-detection correctly prefers frankentorch over fastembed when both available
9. Fallback from frankentorch to fastembed works when frankentorch errors

comments.text:
Verified fix and cleaned up residual unused import.

Root cause: FrankenSQLite `Connection` uses `Rc` (not `Arc`), so it's `!Send`/`!Sync`. 
The old approach of sharing a `claim_lock: Arc<Mutex<()>>` across separate `Storage` 
connections was fundamentally broken — each connection had its own isolated in-memory 
snapshot, so the mutex serialized claim_batch calls but didn't prevent TOCTOU races 
on the underlying data (each connection read stale snapshots independently).

Fix (already applied, verified here):
1. Removed `claim_lock` field and `with_shared_claim_lock()` constructor from PersistentJobQueue
2. Added documentation in `claim_batch` that all calls MUST route through a single 
   PersistentJobQueue instance backed by one Storage connection
3. Replaced broken multi-connection test with channel-dispatcher pattern test 
   (`concurrent_claim_once_through_shared_queue_has_no_double_assignment`) that 
   matches the production pattern (asupersync event loop owns storage)

A machine-readable handoff separates remote optimized compilation from model-bearing execution. No debug-profile transformer inference and no inherited developer cache are admissible.
acceptance_criteria: A committed E2E driver runs required lexical, QualityOnly, FullProgressive, hash-control, hybrid and persisted-restart lanes in fresh processes with FRANKENSEARCH_REQUIRE_SEMANTIC_E2E=1. No fixture/model/lane may skip. Exact verified inputs and optimized executing ELF are recorded. Network denial, timeout/signal handling, CPU/wall/RSS, <=10000 lines, <=8MiB, redaction canaries and artifact upload apply on pass and every failure class. Evidence records source/dirty state, Cargo.lock/toolchain/features/profile, build and executing ELF hashes, model/corpus/qrels/chunker/input-contract/generation hashes, exact command/environment and metrics. PR bounded real-inference and scheduled clean rebuild/restart/rollback lanes both pass reproducibly.

Observed: 17 min elapsed / 7h14m CPU across 66 threads and still going. The CI lane MUST use --release, otherwise it will be disabled by whoever next tunes CI runtime. Documented in the test's module doc.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CONCRETE CI PROVISIONING REQUIREMENT, learned the hard way 2026-07-26 (TealIsland).

This bead will fail in CI if it provisions the model the way this dev host had it provisioned. The real-MiniLM lanes do NOT need "a tokenizer and some weights" — NativeEmbedder::load verifies the FULL frozen artifact set from ModelArtifactManifestV1::minilm_native_frankentorch(), five files, each by size AND sha256, at pinned revision c9745ed1d9f207416be6d2e6f8de32d1f16199bf:

  model.safetensors        90868376  53aa51172d142c89d9012cce15ae4d6cc0ca6895895114379cacb4fab128d9db
  tokenizer.json             466247  be50c3628f2bf5bb5e3a7f17b1f74611b2561a3a27eeab05e5aa30f411572037
  config.json                   612  953f9c0d463486b10a6871cc2fd59f223b2c70184f49815e7efbcab5d8908b41
  special_tokens_map.json       112  303df45a03609e4ead04bc3dc1536d0ab19b5358db685b6f3da123d05ec200e3
  tokenizer_config.json         350  acb92769e8195aabd29b7b2137a9e6d6e25c476a4f15aa4355c233426c61576b

Total 90,868,376 + 467,321 bytes. A cache key for the CI model dir should be the concatenated sha256 set, not the model name — that way the manifest tightening that just invalidated this hosts model dir would invalidate the CI cache too instead of serving a stale partial dir forever.

SECOND, AND MORE IMPORTANT FOR THIS BEADS PURPOSE: FRANKENSEARCH_REQUIRE_SEMANTIC_E2E=1 is necessary but NOT sufficient to prove the semantic lane actually ran. It only converts resolve_model_dir()s soft skip into a panic. resolve_model_dir (treasure_island_e2e.rs:260-296) currently probes for tokenizer.json plus EITHER model_f32.safetensors OR model.safetensors — two of the five artifacts. So a partial model dir passes the guard, the test proceeds, and it dies later inside NativeEmbedder::load with a bare "missing model file: .../config.json". That is exactly what happened here: the guard said "model present, do not skip", and the lane still could not run.

So a CI lane that only sets the env var can still report a confusing mid-test panic rather than an actionable provisioning error. The guard must check the same artifact set the loader checks. I am fixing resolve_model_dir under bd-8w6e to derive its required-file list from the frozen manifest (frankensearch-embed is already a dev-dependency of the facade, Cargo.toml:56, so the manifest is reachable) rather than keeping a second hardcoded list that can drift again. Sequence this bead after that fix so CI inherits the accurate guard.

THIRD: assert positively that the lane executed. Env-var-gated tests that silently return Ok are indistinguishable from tests that ran. Recommend the CI job additionally assert the expected test COUNT (currently 7 with --features quill,native) and fail if any lane reports as filtered/skipped.

title: HNSW d_id vs VectorIndex position mismatch in two_tier.rs search_fast tombstone filter
description:
In two_tier.rs search_fast(), the ANN path filters soft-deleted records via hits.retain(|hit| !self.fast_index.is_deleted(hit.index as usize)). But hit.index is the HNSW d_id (compact 0..hnsw.len()), NOT the VectorIndex position. After tombstone-aware HNSW rebuild (build_from_vector_index skips deleted records), d_ids no longer equal VectorIndex positions.

Example: VectorIndex=[A@0, B@1(deleted), C@2] → HNSW=[A(d_id=0), C(d_id=1)]. If C is later deleted at VectorIndex pos 2, is_deleted(1) checks pos 1 (B, already deleted) instead of pos 2 (C). Fix: store original VectorIndex positions in HNSW, or filter by doc_id lookup instead of index.

Severity: MEDIUM — triggers after HNSW rebuild with pre-existing tombstones, then additional deletions before next rebuild.
close_reason: Already resolved - code at two_tier.rs:271-279 now uses find_index_by_doc_id(&hit.doc_id) for tombstone checks instead of hit.index. The comment at line 271 explicitly notes the d_id vs VectorIndex position divergence.

title: Integrate fast_cmaes for automated search hyperparameter optimization
description:
Integrate fast_cmaes (SIMD-accelerated CMA-ES optimizer, already complete at /dp/fast_cmaes with both Rust library and Python bindings) to automatically tune frankensearch's hand-picked search quality parameters against the test fixture corpus.

MOTIVATION: frankensearch's TwoTierConfig contains ~10 manually chosen constants (blend_factor=0.7, rrf_k=60, candidate budgets, timeouts). These were picked by intuition, not empirical optimization. CMA-ES is a derivative-free evolutionary optimizer ideal for noisy, non-differentiable objective functions in low-dimensional spaces — exactly the profile of search quality metrics like nDCG.

PARAMETERS TO OPTIMIZE (grouped by sensitivity):
- Group A (ranking quality): blend_factor (currently 0.7/0.3), rrf_k (currently 60), reranker_score_threshold
- Group B (budget allocation): initial_candidate_budget, refined_candidate_budget, per-QueryClass budget multipliers (4 values: Empty/Identifier/Short/NL)
- Group C (latency tradeoffs): quality_tier_timeout_ms, fast_only_threshold
- Total: 10-12 continuous parameters, well within CMA-ES sweet spot (<50 dims)

OBJECTIVE FUNCTION:
- Primary metric: nDCG@10 computed over the 25 ground-truth queries in the fixture corpus (bd-3un.38)
- Secondary metrics (logged but not optimized): MAP@10, MRR, Recall@20, P95 latency
- Multi-objective: weighted sum — 0.8 * nDCG@10 + 0.2 * (1 - normalized_p95_latency) to prevent solutions that sacrifice all latency for marginal quality

OVERFITTING PREVENTION (critical with only 120-doc corpus):
- 5-fold cross-validation: split the 25 queries into 5 folds, optimize on 4, validate on held-out fold
- Report both mean CV score and variance across folds
- If CV variance > 0.05, flag the solution as potentially overfit
- Final parameters = median of the 5 per-fold optima (robust to outliers)
- Compare optimized nDCG vs hand-tuned baseline; reject if improvement < 2% (noise floor)

CMA-ES CONFIGURATION:
- Population size: 4 + floor(3 * ln(n_params)) ≈ 11 for 10 params
- Initial sigma: 0.3 (moderate exploration)
- Max generations: 200 (sufficient for 10-dim convergence)
- Seed: fixed (42) for reproducibility; re-run with 3 additional seeds to verify stability
- Use fast_cmaes Rust API directly (not Python bindings) to stay in-process

ARCHITECTURE:
1. New binary: examples/optimize_params.rs (or tools/optimize_params.rs)
2. Loads fixture corpus and ground truth from tests/fixtures/
3. For each CMA-ES candidate parameter vector:
   a. Construct TwoTierConfig from the candidate
   b. Build index over fixture corpus using hash embedder (fast, deterministic)
   c. Run all 25 ground truth queries through TwoTierSearcher
   d. Compute nDCG@10 against ground truth rankings
   e. Return negative nDCG as fitness (CMA-ES minimizes)
4. After convergence: write optimal parameters to data/optimized_params.toml
5. Log full optimization trace to data/optimization_log.jsonl

OUTPUT ARTIFACTS (checked into repo):
- data/optimized_params.toml: optimal parameter values with metadata (fitness, generation, seed, CV scores)
- data/optimization_log.jsonl: per-generation best/mean/worst fitness, sigma, parameter values
- data/optimization_report.md: human-readable summary with before/after nDCG comparison

INTEGRATION WITH TwoTierConfig:
- TwoTierConfig::optimized() constructor loads from data/optimized_params.toml
- TwoTierConfig::default() retains current hand-tuned values as fallback
- Feature flag: none needed — the optimizer is a dev-time tool, not a runtime dependency

LOGGING:
- tracing spans for each generation with fields: gen_number, best_fitness, mean_fitness, sigma, elapsed_ms
- Per-evaluation tracing: query, ndcg_at_10, candidate_params
- Summary log at convergence: total_evaluations, wall_time, improvement_over_baseline
acceptance_criteria:
1. Optimizer binary runs to completion on fixture corpus in <60s
2. Optimized nDCG@10 >= hand-tuned baseline nDCG@10 (no regression)
3. 5-fold CV variance < 0.05 (not overfit)
4. Optimization is fully reproducible: same seed produces identical parameters
5. optimized_params.toml round-trips correctly (load/save/load produces identical config)
6. optimization_log.jsonl is valid JSONL with monotonically improving best_fitness
7. TwoTierConfig::optimized() loads and applies parameters correctly
notes:
TESTING REQUIREMENTS:

Unit tests (in examples/optimize_params.rs or a dedicated test module):
1. Objective function returns valid nDCG in [0,1] for any legal parameter vector
2. Objective function returns 0.0 for degenerate params (rrf_k=0, blend_factor=0)
3. Parameter bounds enforcement: blend_factor in [0,1], rrf_k in [1,200], timeouts > 0
4. Cross-validation fold generation: each query appears in exactly one held-out fold
5. TOML serialization round-trip: TwoTierConfig -> TOML -> TwoTierConfig is lossless
6. Optimization trace JSONL: each line is valid JSON with required fields

E2E test script (tests/e2e_optimize.sh):
1. Run optimizer with --max-generations=5 --seed=42 (fast smoke test)
2. Verify optimized_params.toml was created and is valid TOML
3. Verify optimization_log.jsonl has exactly 5 generation entries
4. Verify optimized nDCG is reported and is a valid float
5. Run optimizer again with same seed, verify output is bit-identical (reproducibility)
6. Load optimized params into TwoTierSearcher, run 3 ground truth queries, verify results are valid

Logging checklist:
- Each generation logs: gen={n} best_fitness={f} mean_fitness={f} sigma={s} elapsed_ms={ms}
- Each evaluation logs at DEBUG: query={q} ndcg={n} params={...}
- Final summary logs: total_evals={n} wall_time={t} baseline_ndcg={b} optimized_ndcg={o} improvement={pct}%
- Errors during evaluation are logged as WARN with full context, not swallowed

title: Epic: Build frankensearch-fast-search (fsfs) as a standalone machine-wide search product
description:

Product vision:
- Default scope: user home directories with configurable roots/exclusions.

  2) Deluxe FrankenTUI mode with powerful interactive search, explanations, and operational introspection inspired by ftui-demo showcase patterns.

- Deterministic, auditable decision-making for expensive operations (embedding generation, scheduling, throttling).
- Evidence-ledger-backed explainability for policy decisions and adaptive mode switches.
- Comprehensive unit/property/integration/e2e/perf/soak validation with rich logging artifacts.

Alien strategy anchors:
- First-principles expected-loss decision contracts (action costs explicit).
- Calibration/guard layers (conformal/e-process style) for adaptive controller safety.
- Strict profile-first optimization loop with one-lever evidence discipline.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
ENRICHMENT — Self-Documenting Context for Workstream 1 (Product Semantics)

## Why This Workstream Exists

fsfs is not just another search tool. It is a machine-wide search product that indexes user home directories — a scope that raises unique challenges:
1. Privacy: users may have sensitive files (credentials, personal docs) that should never appear in search results or logs
2. Cost: indexing everything is prohibitively expensive (embedding a 50K file corpus at quality-tier takes ~107 minutes)
3. Utility: not all files are worth indexing (binary blobs, vendored code, node_modules)
4. Safety: the system makes expensive autonomous decisions (when to embed, when to throttle) that need formal justification

This workstream establishes the DECISION FRAMEWORK that all other workstreams consume. It answers: "Given a file/query/resource state, what should fsfs do and why?"

## Key Outputs
- bd-2hz.1.1: Dual-mode product contract (CLI vs TUI behavior parity)
- bd-2hz.1.2: Expected-loss action matrices (formal cost/benefit for every autonomous decision)
- bd-2hz.1.3: Privacy/redaction boundaries (what never gets indexed, logged, or displayed)
- bd-2hz.1.4: Alien recommendation contracts (calibration/guard layers for adaptive controllers)

## How It Connects to Other Workstreams
- Workstream 2 (corpus discovery) uses the utility scoring from 1.2
- Workstream 3 (indexing) uses the privacy boundaries from 1.3
- Workstream 4 (pressure control) uses the alien contracts from 1.4
