title: Build data-pipeline integration test suite (collectors to storage to aggregation)
description:
TASK: Create an integration test suite that exercises the ops control plane data pipeline in isolation (without the UI). The pipeline flows: frankensearch instance -> collectors (bd-2yu.5.x) -> transport -> ingestion writer (bd-2yu.4.2) -> storage -> aggregation (bd-2yu.4.3) -> query API.

BACKGROUND: bd-2yu.8.2 covers unit tests for individual engines. bd-2yu.8.3 covers full e2e with the UI. But there is no test for the data pipeline layer specifically. Schema/contract drift between collectors and storage, or between storage and aggregation, can cause silent data corruption that unit tests miss and e2e tests may not catch clearly.

MUST INCLUDE:
1. Schema conformance: verify collector output matches ingestion writer expectations
2. End-to-end data flow: inject synthetic events at collector, verify they appear correctly in aggregated form
3. Contract drift detection: type-checked round-trip serialization/deserialization at every pipeline stage
4. Backpressure behavior: verify correct event dropping under load without pipeline corruption
5. Clock skew handling: inject events with out-of-order timestamps, verify aggregation handles gracefully
6. Retention enforcement: verify old events are purged per retention policy
7. Recovery from storage corruption: inject malformed data, verify pipeline continues

TESTING APPROACH:
- Use deterministic simulator (bd-2yu.8.1) to generate synthetic events
- Wire through actual pipeline code (not mocks) with in-memory FrankenSQLite database
- Assert invariants at each pipeline stage
- Run as CI test (< 2 minutes)

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
- Pipeline integration tests catch any schema/contract mismatch introduced by changes to collectors, storage, or aggregation
- Zero data loss under normal operation (verified by event counting)
- Graceful behavior under every tested error condition
acceptance_criteria:
1. Pipeline integration suite covers collector -> transport -> ingestion -> storage -> aggregation -> query-path contracts.

title: Dependency semantics normalization and CI lint gate for bead references
description:
Perform a one-time and then automated ongoing normalization pass over bead dependency semantics.

Problem this addresses:
Many beads reference other bead IDs in descriptions/comments without clearly declaring whether those references are:
- hard prerequisites (must be `blocks` edges)
- soft interactions (should be documented but not blocking)
- informational context only

Work required:
1) Build a reference scanner that extracts bead-id mentions from issue text.
2) For each mention, enforce explicit classification:
   - HARD_DEP: must exist as a dependency edge
   - SOFT_DEP: documented interaction, intentionally non-blocking
   - INFO_REF: context-only mention
3) Add a lint report consumable in CI so new ambiguous references fail quality gates.
4) Backfill existing high-impact beads with explicit SOFT_DEP/HARD_DEP annotations where needed.

This reduces hidden coupling, prevents accidental overblocking/underblocking, and keeps multi-agent execution plans predictable.
acceptance_criteria:
1) A deterministic scanner reports all bead-id references and classifies each as HARD_DEP, SOFT_DEP, or INFO_REF.
2) CI fails when a new reference is unclassified or when HARD_DEP references are missing actual dependency edges.
3) Existing high-centrality beads are backfilled with explicit classification annotations and pass the lint gate.
4) The lint output is concise, machine-readable, and suitable for multi-agent planning workflows.
5) Documentation explains the classification policy with examples and update workflow.
close_reason: Completed dependency-semantics normalization + CI lint gate chain (.1-.7)

title: Write unit and integration tests for incremental FSVI append
description:
Comprehensive test suite for the incremental append-only FSVI index (bd-1hw).

TEST MATRIX:

Unit Tests:
1. append_single_vector: Append one vector, verify it's searchable via top_k_search. Assert WAL file created.
2. append_batch: Append 100 vectors in one batch, verify all searchable. Assert batch is atomic (all-or-nothing on error).
3. append_idempotency: Append same doc_id twice — second should overwrite (or error, depending on policy). Test both policies.
4. wal_persistence: Append vectors, drop VectorIndex, reopen — WAL vectors still searchable.
5. compaction_basic: Append vectors, compact, verify record count = main + WAL, search results unchanged.
6. compaction_threshold: Verify needs_compaction() triggers at correct WAL-to-main ratio.
7. compaction_atomic_swap: During compaction, concurrent search must not see partial state. Use thread barrier.
8. wal_record_count: Verify wal_record_count() accuracy after various append/compact cycles.
9. search_merge_correctness: Main has doc A (score 0.9) and WAL has doc B (score 0.95). Verify B ranks higher.
10. empty_wal_search: Search with empty WAL returns same results as main-only search.

Integration Tests:
11. concurrent_append_and_search: 4 threads appending, 4 threads searching. Verify no corruption (no panics, no missing docs after all threads finish).
12. large_wal_performance: Append 10K vectors to WAL, measure search overhead vs main-only. Assert <10% overhead when WAL is <10% of main.
13. compact_during_search: Start a long search (artificial delay), compact in background. Verify search completes correctly.
14. fsync_durability: Append, kill process (simulate crash), reopen — verify WAL records survived.

Benchmarks:
15. bench_append_single: Latency of single append (target: <100us excluding fsync).
16. bench_append_batch_100: Latency of 100-doc batch append (target: <5ms).
17. bench_search_wal_overhead: Search latency vs WAL size (0%, 1%, 5%, 10%, 20% of main).
18. bench_compaction: Compaction time for various main+WAL sizes.

All tests use the FNV-1a hash embedder for deterministic, fast embeddings. Use tracing::info! for key test events.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The requested test suite is implemented for the target feature or module and wired into normal test commands and CI lanes.
2. Tests cover happy paths, edge and boundary conditions, and failure or degraded scenarios, including concurrency and cancellation where applicable.
3. Tests assert structured logs, metrics, or reason codes so failures are diagnosable without manual reproduction.
4. Test execution is deterministic and reproducible and emits actionable artifacts on failure (fixtures, traces, summaries, replay context).
5. Documented coverage and pass criteria are met, and no flaky behavior is introduced.

title: RELEASE GATE: default Quill flip requires a validated WIN on every frozen QG target and required machine class
description:
BINDING USER PERFORMANCE DECISION FOR THE LIBRARY LEXICAL FLIP. This supersedes the earlier bounded non-inferiority and AllowWithOptimizationDebt proposal. The facade lexical feature and every aggregate that selects it must not flip to Quill until Quill is both conformant and faster or better than the fastest semantically equivalent live Tantivy incumbent on every frozen QG-1 through QG-10 target, every required cell, and every required machine class. MISS, NoDecision, Block, Quarantine, Unsupported, unavailable required hardware, invalid A/A, incomplete provenance, or an unmeasured cell all keep this gate open. No agent may reduce a target, waive a class, substitute a self-speedup, or infer one platform from another without a new explicit user instruction.

Measurement and optimization still proceed anti-paralysis style: run every ready diagnostic or decision cell immediately, retain honest misses and invalid attempts, and start a profile-first running-the-gauntlet-on-your-rust-port lane for every credible loss. That execution policy changes latency to learning, never the release threshold. The flip gate consumes the complete E8 terminal census plus the canonical machine-class registry and verifies target-level victory independently of whether the census has otherwise reached a terminal MISS or Block state.

Every competitive result must bind the fastest screened semantically equivalent Tantivy arm in the same invocation and binary, identical workload/options/resources, both-engine absolutes, raw samples, balanced order, metric-appropriate uncertainty, quantile-specific A/A controls where noisy, exact executable/source/corpus/query/machine provenance, and total conformance. Cross-machine ratios, smoke-scale extrapolation, self-speedups, point estimates without required confidence bounds, and aggregate wins hiding a losing class or tail are inadmissible.
design: Keep three separate machine-readable truths: conformance eligibility, complete E8 evidence census, and this all-target performance-victory release gate. The machine-class registry freezes required classes and per-class cell scope before decision runs. E8 terminal reconciliation may truthfully finish a measurement campaign with MISS, Block, Quarantine, or NoClaim; this release gate remains open unless every required target is a validator-green WIN. A WIN uses the direction and confidence rule frozen by the owning QG contract, never a post-hoc materiality threshold. Required AMD high-core and Apple Silicon cells are first-class and cannot be replaced by x86 VPS evidence. Public speed claims remain a separate citation check, but the atomic facade flip commit depends directly on this gate.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The canonical machine-class registry and executable manifest enumerate every required gate, fixture, state, percentile, scale, thread/core mode, and platform class before the final campaign runs. 2. QG-1 through QG-10 have immutable validator-green artifacts for every required cell with zero unmeasured, omitted, duplicated, mixed-provenance, unsupported, NoDecision, Quarantine, Block, or MISS outcomes. 3. Every numeric target is a WIN under its predeclared confidence rule and direction; all co-primary endpoints pass, including per-class and tail rules, and no weighted aggregate masks a losing query, density, topology, percentile, or platform. 4. Required high-core AMD and Apple Silicon lanes carry class-specific A/A calibration, exact local execution and hardware fingerprints, affinity or observable scheduling facts, thermal/governor/NUMA state, and durability symmetry where applicable. 5. Every result compares Quill against the fastest screened semantically equivalent live Tantivy arm in the same binary and invocation and records both-arm absolutes, raw paired blocks, exact ELF/source/corpus/query identities, and total conformance. 6. Every historical or current loss has a profile-first gauntlet trail with one lever per commit and keep/reject evidence; no self-speedup satisfies a competitive target. 7. The pre-flip orchestrator and CI fail closed on any missing class/cell, weakened target, stale artifact, invalid null, point-only decision, uncited substitution, or non-WIN state. 8. The flip bead, contracts, docs, examples, release notes, and machine-readable feature manifest state this all-target-WIN rule consistently. Closure of this bead is impossible merely because E8 terminal reconciliation or an optimization round ended.

title: Use frankenscipy solvers for score calibration numerical methods
description:
When frankenscipy matures, swap the numerical backends inside the score calibration service (bd-22k) from hand-rolled implementations to frankenscipy's solver portfolio. This is a BACKEND SWAP, not a new feature — the ScoreCalibrator trait and its 4 implementations (Identity, TemperatureScaling, PlattScaling, IsotonicRegression) are defined and implemented by bd-22k. This bead replaces the numerical guts.

WHY SWAP:
bd-22k will initially implement the solvers with straightforward code:
- TemperatureScaling: gradient descent loop for single-parameter NLL minimization
- PlattScaling: basic L-BFGS or gradient descent for 2-parameter logistic fit
- IsotonicRegression: Pool Adjacent Violators (PAV) algorithm (simple, ~50 lines)

These hand-rolled implementations will work but lack:
1. Condition-aware solver selection (frankenscipy's CASP)
2. Convergence diagnostics and stability certificates
3. Numerical edge-case handling (ill-conditioned score distributions, near-singular Hessians)
4. Automatic step-size adaptation and line search strategies

WHAT FRANKENSCIPY PROVIDES:
frankenscipy's Condition-Aware Solver Portfolio (CASP) selects the best algorithm based on runtime conditioning diagnostics:

1. For TemperatureScaling (single-param optimization):
   - frankenscipy::optimize::minimize_scalar(nll, bounds=(0.01, 100.0), method=Auto)
   - CASP auto-selects: Brent's method for well-conditioned, golden section for noisy
   - Convergence certificate: |f(T_{k}) - f(T_{k-1})| < tol with condition number

2. For PlattScaling (2-param optimization):
   - frankenscipy::optimize::minimize(nll, x0=[0.0, 0.0], method=Auto)
   - CASP auto-selects: L-BFGS-B for smooth, Nelder-Mead for noisy
   - Gradient provided analytically: d_nll/da, d_nll/db
   - Hessian conditioning check: log10(cond(H)) > 10 → switch to regularized variant

3. For IsotonicRegression (constrained monotonic fit):
   - frankenscipy::isotonic::IsotonicRegression::fit(scores, labels)
   - PAV algorithm with weighted samples support
   - Produces breakpoint vector for O(log n) lookup at query time
   - Monotonicity is guaranteed by construction (no numerical issues possible)

MIGRATION PATH:
1. bd-22k lands first with hand-rolled solvers (fully functional, tested)
2. This bead adds frankenscipy as an OPTIONAL dependency behind feature flag: `calibration-scipy = ['dep:frankenscipy']`
3. When feature is enabled, ScoreCalibrator::fit() delegates to frankenscipy solvers
4. When feature is disabled, hand-rolled solvers remain (zero regression)
5. Parity tests verify both backends produce equivalent calibration parameters

FEATURE FLAG:
`calibration-scipy = ['dep:frankenscipy']` in frankensearch-fusion/Cargo.toml
- Off by default (frankenscipy is a large dependency)
- The `full` meta-feature should include it when frankenscipy is mature

CRATE PLACEMENT:
frankensearch-fusion/src/calibration.rs (same file as bd-22k's trait + impls)
- Add #[cfg(feature = "calibration-scipy")] blocks for frankenscipy-backed implementations
- The ScoreCalibrator trait interface is unchanged
acceptance_criteria:
1. frankenscipy-backed TemperatureScaling produces T within 1% of hand-rolled solver for same input data
2. frankenscipy-backed PlattScaling produces (a, b) within 1% of hand-rolled solver
3. frankenscipy-backed IsotonicRegression produces identical breakpoints to hand-rolled PAV
4. Calibrated scores from both backends produce identical rankings (same nDCG@10 on fixture queries)
5. CASP diagnostics are logged: solver selected, condition number, convergence iterations
6. Feature flag works: builds without frankenscipy, builds with frankenscipy, both produce correct results
7. Ill-conditioned input (all-identical scores) handled gracefully — solver returns Identity fallback with WARN
8. ECE (Expected Calibration Error) is within 0.01 of hand-rolled backend on fixture corpus
notes: Deferred by backlog harmonization pass. Re-entry criteria: (1) Sprint-1 keystone program bd-1zxn closed, (2) release gate bd-ehuk closed, (3) proof-lane contract bd-bobf has at least one completed exemplar, and (4) concrete EV score >= 2.0 with measured hotspot evidence.

description:
TERMINAL SEMANTIC RECOVERY INTEGRATION. Map typed model, manifest, remote producer trust, vector-space/input/storage identity, generation, ANN provenance, cache, coverage and zero-signal state into one versioned RecoveryPlan across library, facade, fsfs readiness/search/provisioning/index/cache/doctor/output and pinned CASS status/health/doctor/query paths. No string parsing. Model acquired, remotely configured, or loaded never means searchable before a verified producer and compatible nonempty indexed generation exist. Explicit semantic fails closed; hybrid lexical fallback reports requested/realized mode, exact reason, coverage, zero admitted semantic scores and recovery. Human/JSON/stream/ops derive from the same typed value. Central bounded constructors own public diagnostic facts; arbitrary raw Display strings cannot cross terminal-event, JSON, stream, ops, tracing, or telemetry boundaries.

CASS evidence is the active ds7uy.1-.5 split: self-sealed replay journal; resumable source-consistent inactive composite generation build; fixed two-slot authority plus external floor publication/reconcile; direct QualityOnly and independent fast+quality FullProgressive retrieval; higher-sequence rollback; retention eligibility dry-run with zero deletion; manifest-only retained exact-tier reader; readiness RecoveryPlan; and acquire/reindex/retry. Each supplies an exact cross-repo commit receipt. Closure includes facade persisted Treasure proof and one no-mock CASS lifecycle driver with crash/cancel injection at every durable publication boundary, restart, higher-sequence rollback, retained old-reader exactness, cache invalidation so fresh queries cannot retain a superseded generation, and zero destructive collection. Any deletion remains separately authorized and out of scope.
design: Adapters accept typed source state and return the shared RecoveryPlan. Exhaustive mapping tests and golden JSON/human snapshots pin schema/version. Products may add presentation context through central redacting constructors but cannot alter codes, prerequisites, destructiveness or expected postcondition. Raw error Display/source/provider text is local diagnostic input, never wire output. Evidence pins exact FrankenSearch/CASS commits plus schema, model, corpus, document-set, component, generation and authority hashes. Retention proof is dry-run only and deletes nothing.
acceptance_criteria: Every model/manifest/remote-trust/FSVI/identity/topology/generation/ANN/cache/coverage/zero-signal/offline/noninteractive state yields the same stable code and semantically identical plan through library, fsfs and CASS. Golden JSON/human/stream/ops mappings are exhaustive. Public-construction and end-to-end canaries inject credentials, query text, vectors, raw paths, newlines/control characters, provider bodies and oversized errors and prove all terminal/JSON/stream/ops/log/telemetry outputs are bounded and redacted; direct raw Display forwarding is structurally unavailable or rejected. Facade persisted Treasure and CASS no-mock ds7uy.1-.5 lifecycle pass with crash/cancel at each fixed-authority publication boundary, explicit higher-sequence rollback, retained old-reader exactness, retention eligibility dry-run with zero deletion, and superseded generation absent from all new query/index caches. Successful acquire+reindex+retry, producer/space drift, partial/corrupt generation and rollback are covered. Exact commits/schema/model/corpus/document-set/component/generation/authority digests, commands and bounded redacted logs are retained. Destructive collection remains separately authorized and out of scope.

comments.text:
## Fixed (SapphireMoose)

Both defects resolved in crates/frankensearch-tui/src/shell.rs and frame.rs:

1. **Per-frame `.to_vec()` clone removed** — Replaced with direct Rect copies (Rect is Copy, 8 bytes) extracted before the mutable borrow on `cached_layout` ends. The render method now extracts `bc_area`, `content_area`, and `status_area` as `Option<Rect>` / `Rect` upfront.

title: NaN score propagation in search_fast WAL merge path
description: In two_tier.rs search_fast(), the WAL merge path at line 277 computes dot_product_f32_f32(&entry.embedding, query_vec) but does not guard against NaN results. Severity: MEDIUM — requires corrupt WAL data to trigger.

title: Progressive PRF Query Expansion
description:
Implement pseudo-relevance feedback (PRF) query expansion between Phase 1 (Initial) and Phase 2 (Refined) of the TwoTierSearcher. After the fast tier returns initial results, extract the top-k result embeddings and compute a centroid that "nudges" the quality-tier query embedding toward the neighborhood of relevant documents.

## Background

Frankensearch uses a two-tier search architecture: Phase 1 uses fast (smaller) embeddings for initial retrieval, and Phase 2 uses quality (larger) embeddings for refinement. These two embedding models encode different aspects of semantic meaning, and the same query may map to different neighborhoods in each embedding space. PRF bridges this gap by using Phase 1's relevance signal to inform Phase 2's query.

This is an adaptation of the Rocchio algorithm (1971), one of the most well-established techniques in information retrieval, adapted for frankensearch's two-tier neural architecture.

## Algorithm

1. Phase 1 completes with fast-tier results (top-k fast embeddings + RRF scores)
2. Compute centroid of top-k fast embeddings, weighted by RRF score
3. Quality-tier query embedding = alpha * original_quality_embedding + (1-alpha) * centroid
4. Phase 2 uses this expanded embedding for quality-tier search
5. alpha in [0.5, 1.0], default 0.8 (mostly original query, slight nudge toward relevant neighborhood)

### Key Insight

Frankensearch's two-tier design provides a "free" feedback signal: Phase 1 results are fast to compute and provide a relevance neighborhood before Phase 2 even starts. This is unlike traditional PRF which requires a separate retrieval pass.

## Implementation

```rust
pub struct PrfConfig {
    pub enabled: bool,           // Default: false
    pub alpha: f64,              // Interpolation weight (default: 0.8)
    pub top_k_feedback: usize,   // Number of Phase 1 results to use (default: 5)
    pub score_weighted: bool,    // Weight centroid by RRF scores (default: true)
}

pub fn prf_expand(
    original_embedding: &[f32],
    feedback_embeddings: &[(&[f32], f64)],  // (embedding, weight)
    alpha: f64,
) -> Vec<f32>;
```

The `prf_expand` function:
1. Computes the weighted centroid of feedback_embeddings (weight = RRF score if score_weighted, else uniform)
2. Interpolates: result = alpha * original + (1-alpha) * centroid
3. L2-normalizes the result (for cosine similarity compatibility)

## Guard Rails

- Only expand if Phase 1 returns >= min_feedback_docs (default: 3). With fewer feedback documents, the centroid is noisy and may hurt relevance.
- Only expand for NaturalLanguage queries (not Identifier/ShortKeyword). Short/keyword queries don't benefit from PRF because their embedding is already precise.
- Configurable: consumers can disable PRF entirely (enabled=false, the default).
- alpha is clamped to [0.5, 1.0] to prevent the centroid from overwhelming the original query intent.

## Justification

Quality-tier embeddings and fast-tier embeddings live in different embedding spaces. A query that maps cleanly in the fast space may land in a suboptimal neighborhood in the quality space. PRF bridges this gap by using Phase 1's relevance signal to guide Phase 2's query. Empirically, this technique improves recall@10 by 5-15% for ambiguous or multi-faceted queries where the fast and quality embeddings disagree on the relevant neighborhood.

## Dependencies Rationale

- Depends on bd-3un.43 (query classification) because PRF should only activate for NaturalLanguage-classified queries
- Depends on bd-3un.24 (TwoTierSearcher) because it modifies the TwoTierSearcher flow between Phase 1 and Phase 2
- Depends on bd-3un.3 (Embedder trait) because it operates on embedding vectors produced by the Embedder

## Considerations

- Embedding dimensionality: fast and quality embeddings may have different dimensions. PRF operates within the quality embedding space, using Phase 1 results to look up their corresponding quality embeddings (if available) or to project from fast to quality space.
- Centroid quality: if Phase 1 results are poor (low scores), the centroid may be noisy. The alpha parameter mitigates this (0.8 = 80% original query).
- Computational cost: centroid computation is O(k*d) where k=feedback docs, d=embedding dimension. For k=5, d=768, this is ~3840 FP multiplications = <0.1ms.

## Testing

- [ ] Unit: alpha=1.0 produces no expansion (original embedding unchanged within epsilon)
- [ ] Unit: alpha=0.0 produces pure centroid (degenerate case, but mathematically correct)
- [ ] Unit: score-weighted centroid vs uniform centroid produce different results
- [ ] Unit: insufficient feedback docs (< min_feedback_docs) skips expansion
- [ ] Unit: QueryClass guard (only NaturalLanguage triggers expansion)
- [ ] Unit: output embedding is L2-normalized
- [ ] Integration: verify recall improvement on test corpus with clustered documents
- [ ] Benchmark: PRF overhead (centroid computation should be <0.1ms for typical parameters)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
PROJECT VISION: frankensearch is a standalone, reusable Rust crate that extracts the 2-tier hybrid search system currently duplicated across 3 projects (cass, xf, mcp_agent_mail_rust). The name 'frankensearch' reflects its Frankenstein-like assembly from the best parts of each codebase.

KEY INSIGHT (from the X post): The user wanted the best of both worlds — sub-millisecond response time (potion-128M) AND high-quality semantic understanding (MiniLM-L6-v2). Rather than choosing one, the solution is a 2-tier progressive system: show fast results immediately, then upgrade them in the background when the quality model finishes. This creates a smooth UX where results appear instantly and improve within ~150ms.

BAKEOFF RESULTS (motivation for model choices):
- FNV-1a hash: 0.07ms, no semantic meaning (fallback only)
- potion-multilingual-128M: 0.57ms, decent semantics (223x faster than MiniLM)
- all-MiniLM-L6-v2: 128ms, excellent semantics (baseline quality)
- The 223x speed gap between potion and MiniLM is exactly why the 2-tier design exists.

HYBRID SEARCH: Combines lexical (Tantivy BM25) with semantic (vector cosine similarity) via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF, K=60). Documents appearing in both lexical AND semantic results get boosted scores, which empirically produces better results than either alone.

GOAL: Drop-in crate for any Rust project needing local search. Feature-gated so consumers pay only for what they use.

title: Implement model manifest and SHA256 verification
description:
Implement the model manifest system that tracks required model files, their SHA256 checksums, and HuggingFace repo details. This ensures reproducible, verifiable model installations.

pub struct ModelManifest {
    pub id: String,               // e.g., 'all-minilm-l6-v2'
    pub repo: String,             // HuggingFace repo path
    pub revision: String,         // Pinned commit SHA for reproducibility
    pub files: Vec<ModelFile>,    // Required files with checksums
    pub license: String,          // SPDX identifier
}

pub struct ModelFile {
    pub name: String,             // Path in repo (e.g., 'onnx/model.onnx')
    pub sha256: String,           // Expected SHA256 hex string
    pub size: u64,                // Expected file size in bytes
}

pub enum ModelState {
    NotInstalled,
    NeedsConsent,                 // User must approve before download
    Downloading { progress_pct: u8, bytes_downloaded: u64, total_bytes: u64 },
    Verifying,
    Ready,
    Disabled { reason: String },
    VerificationFailed { reason: String },
    UpdateAvailable { current_revision: String, latest_revision: String },
    Cancelled,
}

Key principles (from cass src/search/model_download.rs):
- NO network calls without explicit user consent (consent-gated downloads)
- Placeholder checksum constant: 'PLACEHOLDER_VERIFY_AFTER_DOWNLOAD'
- Production-ready = has_verified_checksums() && has_pinned_revision()
- Atomic installation: download to temp dir, verify, then rename into place

Built-in manifests:
- ModelManifest::minilm_v2() - the baseline quality model
- ModelManifest::potion_128m() - the fast tier model

Verification:
- SHA256 streaming verification during download (sha2 crate)
- Post-install verification on model load
- Version upgrade detection (compare revisions)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
REVISION: Model Manifest and Consent Flow

1. Consent-Gated Downloads:
   The manifest system enforces NO network access without explicit user consent.
   State machine: NotInstalled -> NeedsConsent -> [user approves] -> Downloading -> ...

   Consent mechanisms (in priority order):
   a) Programmatic: ModelManifest::set_consent(true) in code
   b) Environment: FRANKENSEARCH_ALLOW_DOWNLOAD=1
   c) Interactive: prompt on stderr if TTY detected
   d) Config file: frankensearch.toml consent = true

   Without consent, auto_detect() returns HashOnly (hash embedder always works).
   This is critical for CI/CD environments where network access is unexpected.

2. Built-in Manifests:
   Two models ship as compile-time constants:
   - MiniLM-L6-v2: sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2
     SHA256 for model.onnx: [computed at implementation time]
     Total size: ~90MB (5 files)
   - potion-128M: minishlab/potion-base-128M
     SHA256 for model.safetensors: [computed at implementation time]
     Total size: ~32MB (2 files)

3. Manifest Extensibility:
   Users can register custom manifests via:
   ModelManifest::register(ModelManifest { id: "my-model", ... });
   This allows custom embedders to participate in the manifest/verification system.

4. Version Pinning:
   Each manifest includes a HuggingFace revision hash.
   Verification fails if the downloaded files don't match the pinned revision.
   This prevents silent model updates from changing search quality.

5. Verification Performance:
   SHA256 of a 90MB file: ~200ms (streaming, not loaded into memory).
   Verification runs at load time, NOT at every search call.
   Cached verification: write .verified sentinel file after first check.

title: Implement model download system with progress reporting
description:
Implement the model download system that handles fetching model files from HuggingFace with progress reporting, resumable downloads, and atomic installation.

Download pipeline:
1. Check ModelState → if NotInstalled, transition to NeedsConsent
2. On consent, transition to Downloading
3. For each file in manifest:
   a. HTTP GET from HuggingFace CDN with range headers for resume
   b. Stream to temp file with progress callbacks
   c. SHA256 verification during streaming
4. After all files downloaded, verify checksums (Verifying state)
5. Atomic rename from temp dir to final location (Ready state)

Progress reporting:
- AtomicU64 for bytes_downloaded (lock-free progress reads)
- AtomicBool for cancellation
- Callback-based progress: Fn(DownloadProgress) for UI integration
- Rate-limited progress updates (every 100ms or 1% progress)

pub struct DownloadProgress {
    pub file_name: String,
    pub bytes_downloaded: u64,
    pub total_bytes: u64,
    pub files_completed: usize,
    pub files_total: usize,
    pub speed_bytes_per_sec: u64,
    pub eta_seconds: Option<u64>,
}

Network policy: 
- asupersync HTTP client with rustls (no system SSL deps)
- Timeout: 30s connect, 300s total per file
- Retry: 3 attempts with exponential backoff
- User-Agent: 'frankensearch/{version}'

This is behind a 'download' feature flag to keep the core crate network-free.

Reference: cass src/search/model_download.rs (state machine, atomic install)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
REVISION: Model Download System Details

1. Resumable Downloads:
   On network interruption, the partial file is kept (with .part suffix).
   On next attempt, send HTTP Range header to resume from byte offset.
   The streaming SHA256 hasher state is NOT persisted (recompute from start on resume).
   This means: resume is efficient for download, but verification restarts.

2. Atomic Installation:
   Download to: {model_dir}/{model_id}/.download/{file_name}.part
   Complete to: {model_dir}/{model_id}/.download/{file_name}
   After all files verified: atomic rename .download/ to final location
   On failure: .download/ directory is left for retry (not cleaned up)
   On success: .download/ is removed

3. Progress Reporting:
   DownloadProgress struct:
   - bytes_downloaded: u64 (AtomicU64, lock-free)
   - bytes_total: u64
   - speed_bytes_per_sec: f64 (smoothed exponential moving average)
   - eta_seconds: f64
   - is_cancelled: bool (AtomicBool)

   Callback: Box<dyn Fn(DownloadProgress) + Send>
   Rate-limited to max 10 updates/second (avoid flooding UI)
   Default callback: log at INFO with progress bar format

4. Cancellation:

   - User-agent: "frankensearch/{version}" (for HuggingFace rate limiting)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
ALIEN-ARTIFACT ENHANCEMENT (Model Registry & Bakeoff)

## Mathematical Upgrade: From Point Estimates to Bayesian Bakeoff

The current bakeoff infrastructure compares embedders by average NDCG. This is ad-hoc and doesn't account for variance, sample size, or the multiple comparisons problem.

### 1. Bayesian A/B Testing with Beta Posteriors

For each embedder pair (A, B), maintain a Beta posterior:

  // For each query in the bakeoff:
  //   If A's NDCG@10 > B's NDCG@10: A_wins += 1
  //   If B's NDCG@10 > A's NDCG@10: B_wins += 1
  //   If tied: both += 0.5

  P(A better than B) = P(Beta(A_wins+1, B_wins+1) > 0.5)

Decision rule:
  - P(A > B) > 0.95 → declare A the winner (95% Bayesian credibility)
  - P(A > B) < 0.05 → declare B the winner
  - Otherwise → need more queries (continue testing)

This gives a FORMAL stopping criterion — no more arbitrary "run N queries and take the average."

### 2. Multi-Armed Bandit for Model Selection

When multiple embedders are available, use Thompson sampling to select the best one adaptively:

  pub struct EmbedderBandit {
      arms: Vec<(String, Beta)>,  // (embedder_id, Beta posterior)
  }

  impl EmbedderBandit {
      pub fn select_embedder(&self) -> &str {
          // Sample from each Beta posterior, pick highest
          self.arms.iter()
              .max_by(|(_, a), (_, b)| a.sample().partial_cmp(&b.sample()).unwrap())
              .map(|(id, _)| id.as_str())
              .unwrap()
      }
  }

This automatically explores new models while exploiting the best known one. Provable O(sqrt(T log T)) regret.

### 3. e-Values for Anytime-Valid Testing

Use e-values instead of p-values for the bakeoff. e-values support OPTIONAL STOPPING — you can look at results at any time and make valid decisions:

  e_n = product(likelihood_ratio_i for i in 1..n)
  If e_n > 1/alpha, reject H0 at level alpha

This means: you can stop the bakeoff EARLY if one model is clearly better, or CONTINUE if results are ambiguous. Traditional hypothesis testing requires fixed sample sizes.

### 4. FDR Control for Multi-Model Comparisons

When comparing K models pairwise (K*(K-1)/2 comparisons), use the e-BH procedure for False Discovery Rate control:

  1. Compute e-values for all pairwise comparisons
  2. Sort e-values in decreasing order
  3. Apply BH threshold: reject hypothesis i if e_i > K*(K-1)/(2*i*alpha)

This controls the expected proportion of false discoveries at level alpha.

### Implementation Priority

1. Beta posterior A/B testing: add to bakeoff report generation
2. Thompson sampling model selection: add to EmbedderStack
3. e-values: add to bakeoff infrastructure
4. FDR control: add when > 4 models are being compared

title: Implement vector index binary format and I/O
description:
Implement the binary vector index format for storing and loading embeddings. This is the on-disk format that enables memory-mapped vector search.

We should unify the formats from all 3 codebases into a single 'FSVI' (FrankenSearch Vector Index) format:

Binary Format (Little-Endian):

Header (variable length):
  Offset  Size  Field
  0       4     magic: 'FSVI' (4 ASCII bytes)
  4       2     version: u16 (start at 1)
  6       2     embedder_id_len: u16
  8       N     embedder_id: UTF-8 bytes
  8+N     4     dimension: u32
  12+N    4     quantization: u8 (0=f32, 1=f16)
  13+N    3     reserved: [u8; 3]
  16+N    8     record_count: u64
  24+N    8     vectors_offset: u64 (byte offset to vector slab)
  32+N    4     header_crc32: u32

Record Table (fixed-size per record, 16 bytes each):
  doc_id_hash: u64     (FNV-1a hash of doc_id for fast lookup)
  doc_id_offset: u32   (offset into string table)
  doc_id_len: u16      (byte length of doc_id)
  flags: u16           (reserved for doc_type enum, etc.)

String Table:
  Concatenated UTF-8 doc_id strings (referenced by offset+len)

Vector Slab (32-byte aligned):
  record_count × dimension × bytes_per_quant (2 for f16, 4 for f32)

Design decisions:
- f16 quantization by default (2x memory savings, minimal quality loss)
- Memory-mapped via memmap2 for zero-copy access
- 32-byte aligned vector slab for SIMD (AVX2 alignment)
- CRC32 header checksum for corruption detection
- Sorted by doc_id_hash for binary search lookup

API:

pub struct VectorIndex {
    mmap: Mmap,               // Memory-mapped file
    metadata: VectorMetadata,
    record_count: usize,
    dimension: usize,
}

impl VectorIndex {
    pub fn open(path: &Path) -> SearchResult<Self>;
    pub fn create(path: &Path, embedder_id: &str, dimension: usize) -> SearchResult<VectorIndexWriter>;
    pub fn record_count(&self) -> usize;
    pub fn dimension(&self) -> usize;
    pub fn embedder_id(&self) -> &str;
    pub fn vector_at_f16(&self, index: usize) -> &[f16];
    pub fn vector_at_f32(&self, index: usize) -> Vec<f32>;
    pub fn doc_id_at(&self, index: usize) -> &str;
}

pub struct VectorIndexWriter {
    file: BufWriter<File>,
    dimension: usize,
    count: u64,
}

impl VectorIndexWriter {
    pub fn write_record(&mut self, doc_id: &str, embedding: &[f32]) -> SearchResult<()>;
    pub fn finish(self) -> SearchResult<()>;
}

Reference formats:
- cass: CVVI (src/search/vector_index.rs, 70-byte rows with message metadata)
- xf: XFVI (src/vector.rs, variable records with doc_type)
- agent-mail: planned AMVI (simplified from XFVI)

Our format (FSVI) is a clean generalization that doesn't bake in domain-specific fields.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
VECTOR INDEX FORMAT DESIGN: The FSVI format is a deliberate generalization of the three existing formats:
- CVVI (cass): 70-byte rows with domain-specific fields (MessageID, AgentID, etc.)
- XFVI (xf): variable records with doc_type enum (tweet/like/dm/grok)
- AMVI (agent-mail): simplified from XFVI

FSVI strips all domain-specific fields. The principle: frankensearch stores (doc_id, embedding) pairs. Any domain metadata belongs in the consumer's own storage. This keeps the index format universal.

Key design choice — f16 by default: 
- 384-dim f16: 768 bytes per doc (vs 1536 for f32) = 50% memory savings
- Quality loss from f16 quantization is < 1% on cosine similarity benchmarks
- Memory-mapped f16 means the OS page cache holds 2x more vectors
- For 100K docs × 384 dims: 73MB (f16) vs 147MB (f32)

The string table design (separate from records) enables fixed-size record entries for binary search lookups while supporting variable-length doc IDs.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
REVISION (review pass 2 - cross-codebase verification):

1. EMBEDDER REVISION FIELD MISSING: The FSVI header must include an embedder_revision field (variable-length UTF-8 string, like embedder_id). This tracks the model's pinned commit SHA (e.g., "c9745ed1d9f207416be6d2e6f8de32d1f16199bf" for MiniLM). Purpose: when a model is updated, the revision changes, and the index must be rebuilt. Without this, stale indices silently return degraded results.

Updated header layout:
  8+N     2     embedder_rev_len: u16
  10+N    M     embedder_revision: UTF-8 bytes
  (adjust all subsequent offsets by M+2)

Reference: cass CVVI header has EmbedderRevision (u16 len + bytes). This was in the original format but was accidentally omitted from the FSVI design.

2. FSYNC ON SAVE: VectorIndexWriter::finish() must call fsync on the file AND fsync the parent directory for write durability. Reference: cass vector_index.rs sync_dir() at line 1538. This prevents data loss on power failure.

3. VECTOR ALIGNMENT: The vector slab must be 32-byte aligned (VECTOR_ALIGN_BYTES = 32) for AVX2 SIMD. Add padding between string table and vector slab as needed.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
EXTREME OPTIMIZATION ENHANCEMENT (FSVI Vector Index Format)

## Profile-Informed I/O and Memory Optimization

### Opportunity Matrix

| Hotspot                    | Impact | Confidence | Effort | Score |
|----------------------------|--------|------------|--------|-------|
| 64-byte cache alignment    | 3      | 5          | 1      | 15.0  |
| madvise(MADV_SEQUENTIAL)   | 4      | 5          | 1      | 20.0  |
| Huge pages (2MB THP)       | 3      | 4          | 1      | 12.0  |
| Vectored write (writev)    | 3      | 3          | 2      | 4.5   |
| fsync strategy             | 2      | 5          | 1      | 10.0  |

### 1. madvise for Sequential Scan (Score: 20.0, MUST DO)

The vector search does a sequential scan through the entire mmap. Tell the OS:

  // After opening the mmap:
  #[cfg(unix)]
  unsafe {
      libc::madvise(
          mmap.as_ptr() as *mut libc::c_void,
          mmap.len(),
          libc::MADV_SEQUENTIAL,
      );
  }

This enables aggressive readahead — the kernel will prefetch pages before we need them. Measured impact: 2-3x throughput improvement for sequential scans on cold caches.

NOTE: This requires `unsafe`. Since the project forbids unsafe_code, use the memmap2 crate's `advise()` method if available, or document this as a future optimization if memmap2 doesn't expose it safely. Alternative: the `region` crate provides safe madvise wrappers.

SAFE ALTERNATIVE: memmap2::MmapOptions::new().populate() will pre-fault all pages, and memmap2::Mmap::advise(Advice::Sequential) provides a safe wrapper for MADV_SEQUENTIAL in recent versions. Check memmap2 API.

### 2. 64-Byte Cache Line Alignment (Score: 15.0)

Current spec says 32-byte alignment for vector slab. Modern CPUs use 64-byte cache lines. Misaligned vector access causes 2 cache line loads per vector start:

  // In FSVI header:
  vectors_offset: round_up_to(header_size + records_size + strings_size, 64)

Change: "32-byte aligned" → "64-byte aligned" in the FSVI format spec. This is a one-line change with measurable impact on scan performance.

### 3. Huge Pages for Large Indices (Score: 12.0)

For indices > 100MB, transparent huge pages (2MB pages) reduce TLB misses by 512x:

  // When creating the mmap:
  #[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
  {
      libc::madvise(ptr, len, libc::MADV_HUGEPAGE);
  }

For a 100K-doc × 384-dim f16 index (~73MB), this reduces TLB misses from ~18K to ~36. Each TLB miss costs ~100 cycles on modern CPUs.

SAFE ALTERNATIVE: Set the system's transparent_hugepages to "madvise" mode and let memmap2 use MAP_HUGETLB flag if available. Or simply document that sysadmins should enable THP for large indices.

### 4. Write Performance: Buffered + Vectored I/O

For index building, use BufWriter with a large buffer (256KB instead of default 8KB), and batch writes:

  let writer = BufWriter::with_capacity(256 * 1024, file);

For the final vector slab write, if all vectors are already in memory (they are, during batch embedding), use a single write() call for the entire slab rather than per-record writes. This reduces syscall overhead from N to 1.

### 5. Isomorphism Proof

- Cache alignment: no data change, only padding
- madvise: kernel hint only, no data change
- Huge pages: memory mapping only, no data change
- Buffer size: same bytes written, just fewer syscalls
- All: sha256(index_file) identical before/after

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
REVIEW FIX — FSVI binary format header reconciliation and alignment decision:

1. CANONICAL HEADER LAYOUT (reconciling body + revision, single source of truth):

   Offset  Size  Field                    Description
   ──────  ────  ─────                    ───────────
   0       4     magic: [u8; 4]           b"FSVI"
   4       2     version: u16             Format version (1)
   6       2     dimension: u16           Vector dimension (e.g., 384)
   8       1     quantization: u8         0=f32, 1=f16, 2=int8, 3=int4 (extensible for bd-qtx)
   9       1     embedder_id_len: u8      Length of embedder_id string (N)
   10      N     embedder_id: [u8; N]     UTF-8 embedder identifier
   10+N    1     embedder_rev_len: u8     Length of embedder_revision string (M)
   11+N    M     embedder_rev: [u8; M]    UTF-8 embedder revision hash
   11+N+M  3     reserved: [u8; 3]        Padding to 4-byte boundary (zeros)
   14+N+M  8     record_count: u64        Number of vectors stored
   22+N+M  4     header_crc32: u32        CRC32 of all preceding header bytes

   Total header size: 26 + N + M bytes (variable, typically ~60-80 bytes)

   After header:
   - Record table: record_count entries of { doc_id_offset: u32, doc_id_len: u16 }
   - String table: concatenated doc_id strings (UTF-8)
   - Vector slab: record_count × dimension × element_size contiguous vectors

2. ALIGNMENT DECISION: 64-byte (cache line) alignment for the vector slab.

   The vector slab start offset is padded to the next 64-byte boundary after the string table. This ensures:
   - SIMD loads (f32x8 = 32 bytes) never cross cache line boundaries
   - mmap access patterns benefit from aligned pages
   - No unsafe needed — the alignment is in the file format, not pointer arithmetic

   vector_slab_offset = (string_table_end + 63) & !63  // Round up to 64-byte boundary

   Padding bytes between string table and vector slab are filled with zeros.

3. FULL-FILE CHECKSUM: Add an optional footer checksum for the vector slab:

   After the last vector:
   - slab_crc32: u32 — CRC32 of the entire vector slab

   This is OPTIONAL (checked only when config.verify_slab_integrity == true) because:
   - CRC32 of a 73MB slab (100K×384×f16) takes ~50ms
   - For typical usage (trusted local files), header CRC is sufficient
   - For untrusted files or after crash, enable slab verification

   When bd-3w1.7 (RaptorQ repair) is enabled, the .fec sidecar provides stronger integrity guarantees, making slab CRC redundant.

4. TEST REQUIREMENTS:
   - Round-trip: write index → read back → all vectors match within quantization tolerance
   - CRC32 verification: correct file passes, 1-byte corruption in header detected
   - Slab CRC (when enabled): 1-byte corruption in vector slab detected
   - Dimension mismatch: open file with wrong expected dimension → clear error
   - Embedder ID mismatch: open file with wrong embedder → clear warning (not error, for migration)
   - Empty index (0 records): writes and reads correctly
   - Large index (100K records): round-trip without data loss
   - f16 quantization fidelity: max |f32_original - f16_roundtrip| < 0.001 for typical embedding values
   - 64-byte alignment: verify vector_slab_offset % 64 == 0
   - Memory-mapped access: mmap the file, read vectors, verify correctness

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
PERFORMANCE: This is the hottest inner loop in the entire search pipeline. The SIMD dot product is called once per stored vector per query. For a 10K-document index with 384-dim embeddings, that's 10,000 dot products of 384 floats each.

wide::f32x8 is the right choice because:
1. Portable: works on x86 (SSE2/AVX2) and ARM (NEON) without #[cfg] branches
2. Safe: no unsafe code needed (wide handles the intrinsics)
3. Fast: 8-wide parallelism reduces loop iterations by 8x
4. Simple: the API is just multiply + horizontal sum

The f16→f32 conversion before SIMD multiply is a necessary cost. f16 SIMD isn't widely supported on CPU. The 2 bytes per dimension (vs 4 for f32) saves 50% memory, which matters when the entire index is memory-mapped.

Benchmark baseline: 384-dim f16×f32 dot product should be < 2μs.

comments.text:
ASUPERSYNC MIGRATION — LIGHT REVISION (rayon RETAINED for data parallelism):

Rayon is RETAINED for brute-force top-k vector search. This is the correct decision because:
1. Vector dot products are CPU-bound, embarrassingly parallel data
2. Rayon's work-stealing scheduler is optimal for this pattern
3. asupersync handles task/structured concurrency; rayon handles data parallelism
4. These compose: an asupersync task can use rayon internally for CPU-bound work

No changes to the core algorithm. The only addition:

ADDITION: When called from an asupersync context, the caller should use cx.checkpoint() BEFORE and AFTER the rayon parallel search to respect cancellation boundaries:

  pub async fn search_top_k(cx: &Cx, index: &VectorIndex, query: &[f32], k: usize) -> asupersync::Result<Vec<VectorHit>> {
      cx.checkpoint()?;  // Cancel check before CPU-bound work
      let results = rayon_search(index, query, k);  // Rayon data parallelism (synchronous)
      cx.checkpoint()?;  // Cancel check after CPU-bound work
      Ok(results)
  }

NOTE: rayon parallel_iter runs synchronously from the caller's perspective — it just uses multiple threads internally. This means the asupersync task is "blocked" during the rayon work, but that's fine because:
1. The rayon work completes in <15ms for 10K vectors
2. cx.checkpoint() on either side provides cancel boundaries
3. For very large indices (100K+), consider splitting into asupersync tasks that each use rayon on a chunk

  - > 500K documents: HNSW required (brute-force exceeds latency budget)

The TwoTierSearcher should auto-select based on index size:
  if index.record_count() > hnsw_threshold { use HNSW } else { use brute-force }
  hnsw_threshold configurable via TwoTierConfig, default 50_000

HNSW build time:
  - 50K docs x 384d: ~5 seconds (one-time cost during index build)
  - 100K docs x 384d: ~12 seconds
  - Build happens in IndexBuilder, not at search time

HNSW persistence:
  - Save to {data_dir}/vector.fast.hnsw and vector.quality.hnsw
  - Load is memory-mapped, instant startup
  - Rebuild if VectorIndex changes (detected by record count or hash mismatch)

Testing: Compare HNSW vs brute-force results for recall measurement.
For top-10 search on 50K docs with ef_search=100: expect recall >= 0.95.
Include in benchmarks (bd-3un.33) for regression tracking.

Note: This is P3 and feature-gated behind 'ann'. The core frankensearch
experience works perfectly without it. Add when scale demands it.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
ALIEN-ARTIFACT ENHANCEMENT (Score Normalization)

## Mathematical Upgrade: From Min-Max to Copula-Based Score Combination

Min-max normalization is the most basic approach and has known failure modes. The alien-artifact approach uses copula theory for principled score combination.

### Problem with Min-Max

Min-max normalization maps scores to [0,1] but:
1. Is sensitive to outliers (one extreme score compresses all others)
2. Destroys distributional information (BM25 scores are roughly Gaussian; cosine similarities are Beta-distributed)
3. Maps different distributions to the same [0,1] range, making them "look similar" when they aren't

### 1. Rank-Based Copula Transform (Recommended Upgrade)

Transform each score set to a uniform distribution via rank transform, then to standard normal:

  fn copula_normalize(scores: &[f32]) -> Vec<f32> {
      // Step 1: Rank transform → Uniform[0,1]
      let ranks = rank_transform(scores);  // ties get averaged ranks
      let uniform: Vec<f32> = ranks.iter().map(|&r| r / (scores.len() as f32 + 1.0)).collect();

      // Step 2: Probit transform → Normal(0,1)
      let normal: Vec<f32> = uniform.iter().map(|&u| probit(u)).collect();
      normal
  }

This preserves the RANKING within each source while making scores comparable across sources. The probit (inverse normal CDF) ensures Gaussian scores, which behave well under linear combination.

### 2. Empirical Bayes Shrinkage for Small Result Sets

When a source returns few results (< 20), min-max normalization is noisy. Apply James-Stein shrinkage toward the grand mean:

  shrunk_score = grand_mean + shrinkage_factor × (raw_score - grand_mean)
  shrinkage_factor = 1 - (n-2) × σ² / Σ(xᵢ - x̄)²

This is provably better than raw scores (dominates in mean squared error for n ≥ 3). It prevents small result sets from producing extreme normalized scores.

### 3. When to Use Which

| Scenario                        | Method              | Why                                     |
|---------------------------------|---------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| RRF fusion                      | None needed         | RRF is rank-based, doesn't use scores   |
| Two-tier blending               | Copula + shrinkage  | Comparing different embedding spaces    |
| Reranker integration            | Min-max is fine     | Same model, same score distribution     |
| Cross-model comparison (bakeoff)| Copula              | Different models, different distributions|

### 4. Keep Min-Max as Default

The copula transform is strictly better but adds complexity. Keep min-max as the default implementation, provide copula_normalize as an opt-in alternative:

  pub enum NormalizationMethod {
      MinMax,           // Simple, fast, good enough for most cases
      CopulaNormal,     // Principled, handles distributional differences
      JamesSteinShrink, // For small result sets (< 20 items)
      None,             // Raw scores (for RRF which doesn't need normalization)
  }

Note: RRF does NOT depend on normalization (rank-based fusion). This was already correctly identified in the review. The normalization improvements apply to the BLENDING step (bd-3un.21) where we combine fast and quality scores.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
REVIEW FIX — z-score edge case and test requirements:

1. Z-SCORE UNDEFINED FOR ZERO STDEV: When all scores are identical, standard deviation = 0, and z-score division produces NaN/Inf. 

   RESOLUTION: If stdev < epsilon (1e-10), skip normalization and assign all scores 0.5 (midpoint). This handles:
   - Single result (stdev = 0)
   - All identical scores (stdev = 0)
   - Near-identical scores (stdev ≈ 0, numerical instability)

2. NORMALIZATION METHODS: Clarify the available methods and when each is used:
   - MinMax: (score - min) / (max - min) → [0, 1]. Used for BM25 scores (unbounded).
   - Z-score: (score - mean) / stdev → approximately [-3, 3], then clamp to [0, 1]. Alternative.
   - None: Pass-through for scores already in [0, 1] (e.g., cosine similarity).
   Default: MinMax for BM25 (lexical), None for cosine (semantic).

3. TEST REQUIREMENTS:
   - MinMax: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] → [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]
   - MinMax single element: [42.0] → [1.0] (or 0.5, define the convention)
   - MinMax identical scores: [3.0, 3.0, 3.0] → [0.5, 0.5, 0.5]
   - Z-score zero stdev: all same scores → all 0.5
   - Z-score normal: verify output mean ≈ 0.5 for symmetric distributions
   - None pass-through: scores unchanged
   - NaN handling: NaN scores in input → handled gracefully (filtered or mapped to 0.0)
   - Ordering preserved: normalization does not change relative order of scores

  Message: "Reranking failed for model {model_id}: {source}"

  Message: "Query parse error at position {position}: {suggestion}"

SearchError::ConfigError { field: String, value: String, reason: String }
  Message: "Invalid config {field}={value}: {reason}"
  Recovery: "Check TwoTierConfig documentation for valid values"

SearchError::IoError(std::io::Error)
  Message: "I/O error: {0}"
  Recovery: "Check file permissions and disk space"

SearchError::TimeoutError { operation: String, elapsed_ms: u64, limit_ms: u64 }
  Message: "{operation} timed out after {elapsed_ms}ms (limit: {limit_ms}ms)"
  Recovery: "Increase timeout in TwoTierConfig, or reduce query complexity"

Design principle: errors should guide the user to a solution, not just report a failure.
The TwoTierSearcher should catch transient errors and degrade gracefully
(EmbeddingError -> fall back to hash, RerankerError -> skip reranking, TimeoutError -> yield Initial).
Only IndexNotFound and ConfigError should prevent search from starting at all.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
RRF ALGORITHM CONTEXT: Reciprocal Rank Fusion was introduced by Cormack et al. (2009) and has become the standard for combining ranked lists from different retrieval systems.

Why K=60: The K parameter controls how much weight is given to high-ranked vs lower-ranked results. K=60 is the empirically optimal value from the original paper and has been independently validated across many IR systems. Higher K values make the scores more uniform (less distinction between ranks); lower K values amplify the importance of being highly ranked.

Why RRF over alternatives:
- Simple: no training data or score calibration needed
- Robust: works well even when score distributions differ wildly (BM25 scores vs cosine similarities)
- Principled: theoretically grounded in rank aggregation
- Proven: used in production at Elastic, Pinecone, Vespa, etc.

The candidate multiplier (3x) is important: if the user wants 10 results, we fetch 30 from each source. This ensures good coverage for docs that might rank differently across sources.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
REVISION (review pass 2 - cross-codebase verification):

1. DETERMINISTIC TIE-BREAKING: The RRF output must use a strict multi-level sort for reproducible results across runs. From xf hybrid.rs and agent-mail fusion.rs:

Sorting chain for FusedHit (ALL levels must be applied):
  Level 1: rrf_score DESCENDING (with epsilon=1e-9 for float comparison)
  Level 2: in_both_sources bonus (true > false) -- docs in both lexical+semantic rank higher on tie
  Level 3: lexical_score DESCENDING (if available, with epsilon comparison)
  Level 4: doc_id ASCENDING (absolute determinism -- string comparison)

This 4-level chain ensures that:
- Results are reproducible across runs (no HashMap iteration order dependency)
- Equal-RRF-score docs are ordered by which had better lexical coverage
- Final doc_id tiebreak prevents any residual ordering ambiguity

2. RANK CONVENTION: Use 0-based ranks internally with the formula:
   score(doc) = 1.0 / (K + rank + 1.0)
   This is equivalent to agent-mail's 1-based convention: 1.0 / (K + rank_1based)
   Document this equivalence explicitly so implementors don't get confused.

3. DEDUPLICATION KEY: After fusion, deduplicate by doc_id. If the same doc_id appears in both sources, its scores are summed (not duplicated). The FusedHit should track both source ranks for explainability.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
ALIEN-ARTIFACT & OPTIMIZATION ENHANCEMENT (RRF Fusion)

## Mathematical Upgrade: From Ad-Hoc RRF to Principled Rank Aggregation

Current design uses fixed K=60 RRF. This works, but there's a richer mathematical framework from social choice theory and probabilistic rank aggregation that would make this genuinely alien-artifact quality.

### 1. Plackett-Luce Rank Aggregation (replaces ad-hoc K constant)

RRF's 1/(K+rank) is actually a special case of the Plackett-Luce model for rank aggregation. The PL model assigns probability to a ranking π as:

  P(π) = ∏ᵢ wᵢ / (Σⱼ≥ᵢ wⱼ)

Where wᵢ are per-item "worth" parameters. When we set wᵢ = 1/(K+rankᵢ), we recover RRF. But the PL framework lets us LEARN optimal weights from implicit feedback (clicks, dwell time), giving us adaptive fusion that improves with usage.

Implementation: Start with RRF (K=60) as the uninformative prior. As user interactions accumulate, update PL weights via MM algorithm (minorization-maximization). This converges in O(n·log n) per update and gives provably optimal rank aggregation under the PL model.

### 2. Kemeny Distance for Fusion Quality Monitoring

Instead of just Kendall's tau for rank correlation (already in bd-3un.21), use Kemeny distance to measure how much the fused ranking deviates from each source. Kemeny distance is the MINIMUM number of pairwise swaps to transform one ranking into another. This gives a principled metric for:
- Detecting when lexical and semantic rankings diverge wildly (→ query is ambiguous)
- Monitoring whether fusion is actually helping (→ average Kemeny distance should decrease)

### 3. Conformal Prediction Sets for Score Calibration

Wrap RRF scores in conformal prediction sets to provide distribution-free coverage guarantees:

  P(doc_relevance ∈ Ĉ(score)) ≥ 1 - α

This requires a calibration set (ground truth relevance judgments for a sample of queries), but provides FORMAL guarantees that the score-to-relevance mapping is calibrated. No distributional assumptions needed.

### 4. Optimal K via Bayesian Online Learning

Instead of fixed K=60, maintain a Gamma(α,β) posterior over K, updated by implicit relevance signals. The posterior predictive gives E[K] = α/β which adapts per-query-class:
- Short queries (1-2 words): may benefit from higher K (more uniform weighting)
- Long queries (5+ words): may benefit from lower K (sharper top-heavy weighting)

### Performance Optimization: Parallel RRF with Sharded HashMap

For large result sets (1000+ from each source), the HashMap-based fusion becomes the bottleneck. Use a sharded HashMap (DashMap or 16 Mutex<HashMap>) partitioned by doc_id hash. Each shard can be updated independently. For the common case (< 300 results per source), the overhead isn't worth it, so add a threshold check.

### Implementation Priority

1. Implement standard RRF first (as designed) — this is correct and well-tested
2. Add Kemeny distance monitoring alongside Kendall's tau — pure addition, no API change
3. Add adaptive K via Beta posterior — simple addition with env var fallback
4. Add Plackett-Luce upgrade path — optional, behind feature flag

These upgrades make the fusion system formally principled while keeping the simple RRF as the always-correct baseline.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
CORRECTNESS NOTE: RRF Score Semantics and Edge Cases

1. Zero-Based Rank Convention Documentation:
   The formula 1/(K + rank + 1) with 0-based ranks means rank=0 gives score 1/(K+1).
   For K=60: rank 0 -> 1/61 = 0.01639, rank 1 -> 1/62 = 0.01613.
   This MUST be documented prominently because off-by-one here silently degrades quality.
   The +1 in the denominator is because the original RRF paper uses 1-based ranks: 1/(K+r).
   With 0-based ranks, this becomes 1/(K+r+1) to produce identical scores.

2. Score Summation for Multi-Source Documents:
   When a document appears in both lexical and semantic results, its RRF scores are SUMMED.
   This means multi-source docs get up to 2x the score of single-source docs.
   This is the standard RRF formulation and is correct -- being retrieved by multiple
   systems is strong evidence of relevance.

3. Dedup Semantics:
   Documents are deduped by doc_id (String equality). When a duplicate is found,
   scores are summed into the first occurrence. The HashMap insert-or-add pattern
   must use entry().and_modify().or_insert() for correctness.

4. Empty Input Handling:
   - Both lists empty -> return empty results
   - One list empty -> return the non-empty list's RRF scores only
   - Both lists have same single doc -> sum both contributions

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
ALIEN-ARTIFACT & OPTIMIZATION ENHANCEMENT (Two-Tier Blending)

## Mathematical Upgrade: From Fixed Blend Factor to Bayesian Adaptive Blending

Current design uses a fixed 0.7 blend factor. This is a reasonable starting point but leaves significant quality on the table. The alien-artifact approach uses online Bayesian learning to adapt the blend factor per query characteristics.

### 1. Beta-Bernoulli Adaptive Blend Weight

Model the "quality model agrees with ground truth" as a Bernoulli trial. Maintain Beta(α,β) posterior, initialized as Beta(7, 3) to encode the 0.7 prior:

  P(quality_is_better | data) ~ Beta(α + successes, β + failures)
  E[blend_factor] = α / (α + β)

After each query with implicit feedback (click on result = success for the scoring system that ranked it higher), update the posterior. The blend factor naturally adapts:
- When quality consistently outperforms fast → α grows → blend_factor → 1.0
- When quality adds noise (e.g., domain mismatch) → β grows → blend_factor → 0.5

This is a CONJUGATE prior, so updates are O(1) with no MCMC needed.

### 2. Thompson Sampling for Exploration-Exploitation

Rather than always using E[blend_factor], occasionally SAMPLE from Beta(α,β) to explore:

  blend = sample(Beta(α, β))

This automatically balances exploitation (use best known blend) with exploration (try different blends to learn faster). Thompson sampling is provably optimal in the Bayesian regret sense.

### 3. Evidence Ledger for Blend Decisions

For every search query, log a structured evidence entry:

  {
    query_hash: u64,
    fast_ndcg: f32,
    quality_ndcg: f32,
    blended_ndcg: f32,
    blend_factor_used: f32,
    rank_correlation: f32,  // Kendall's tau between fast and quality
    quality_latency_ms: u64,
    decision_reason: "bayesian_posterior" | "fixed_default" | "fast_only_timeout"
  }

This provides complete explainability — you can always show exactly WHY the blend factor was what it was.

### 4. Formal Regret Bound

Under the Beta-Bernoulli model with Thompson sampling, the expected regret after T queries is bounded by:

  E[Regret(T)] ≤ O(√(T · log T))

This is a formal guarantee that the blend factor converges to optimal at a known rate.

### 5. Performance: Zero-Overhead Adaptive Blending

The Beta posterior is just two floats (α, β). Sampling from Beta requires one call to the beta distribution RNG (< 1μs). The overhead vs. fixed 0.7 is literally unmeasurable.

The blend_factor computation itself is the same multiply-add — only the WEIGHT changes.

### Implementation in bd-3un.21

Add to the blend module:

  pub struct AdaptiveBlender {
      alpha: AtomicF32,  // Beta posterior param (success count + prior)
      beta: AtomicF32,   // Beta posterior param (failure count + prior)
      min_samples: usize, // Don't adapt until N queries observed (default: 50)
  }

  impl AdaptiveBlender {
      pub fn new() -> Self { Self { alpha: 7.0, beta: 3.0, min_samples: 50 } }
      pub fn blend_factor(&self) -> f32 { self.alpha / (self.alpha + self.beta) }
      pub fn update(&self, quality_was_better: bool) { ... }
  }

The fixed 0.7 fallback is the zero-observation case (Beta(7,3) prior). Full backward compatibility.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
CORRECTNESS NOTE: Two-Tier Blend Scoring for Partial Coverage

Design decision documentation for missing score handling:

The blend function uses 0.0 for missing scores: if a document has a fast_score but no
quality_score, its blended score = fast_score * (1-blend_factor) + 0.0 * blend_factor.

This is INTENTIONAL and CORRECT in the two-tier pipeline because:

1. Phase 1 only computes quality embeddings for the top N candidates from Phase 0.
2. Documents outside top N never enter the blend function.
3. Within the top N, all documents have fast scores. A missing quality score means
   the quality model couldn't process it (e.g., timeout, error).
4. Using 0.0 for missing quality scores penalizes failed-to-embed docs, which is
   the correct conservative behavior (we don't know their quality score).

Alternative considered and rejected:
- Imputing missing quality scores from fast scores (e.g., quality = fast * 0.8)
  This would be an unjustified assumption about score correlation.
- Keeping fast score unchanged for missing quality
  This would bypass the blend entirely, giving fast-only docs an unfair advantage
  when blend_factor > 0.5 (which is the default at 0.7).

IMPORTANT: The blend function MUST document this behavior clearly with an example
in its doc comment showing the scoring math for a doc with missing quality score.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
REVIEW FIX — AtomicF32 does not exist, and test requirements:

1. AtomicF32 DOES NOT EXIST IN STD: If the body references AtomicF32 for the blend weight, this type doesn't exist in Rust's std library. Options:
   a) Use AtomicU32 with f32::to_bits() / f32::from_bits() bit-cast pattern (same as bd-21g's AtomicF64 fix)
   b) Use asupersync::sync::Mutex<f32> (simpler, cancel-aware)
   c) Use a regular f32 behind Arc<asupersync::sync::RwLock<TwoTierConfig>> — the blend weight comes from config

   RESOLUTION: Option (c) — the blend weight is part of TwoTierConfig, which is already behind a shared reference. No atomic needed. If hot-path performance requires avoiding the lock, use option (a):
   let bits = AtomicU32::load(Ordering::Relaxed);
   let weight = f32::from_bits(bits);

2. BLEND FORMULA: Clarify the canonical formula:
   final_score = alpha * quality_score + (1 - alpha) * fast_score
   where alpha = config.quality_weight (default 0.7)
   
   For documents only in one source:
   - Only in fast: final_score = (1 - alpha) * fast_score
   - Only in quality: final_score = alpha * quality_score
   This naturally penalizes single-source results.

3. TEST REQUIREMENTS:
   - Alpha=0.7: quality_score=1.0, fast_score=0.5 → blended = 0.7*1.0 + 0.3*0.5 = 0.85
   - Alpha=1.0: only quality score matters
   - Alpha=0.0: only fast score matters
   - Single-source (fast only): correct penalty applied
   - Single-source (quality only): correct penalty applied
   - Both sources same score: blended = original score
   - Ordering: higher quality scores promote documents
   - NaN scores: handled gracefully (skip or default to 0.0)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
REVISION: TwoTierIndex Implementation Details

1. Cache Invalidation Strategy:
   - OnceLock means indices are loaded once and stay resident
   - Invalidation via TwoTierIndex::reload() which replaces the OnceLock contents
   - On index rebuild: writer creates new files with .tmp suffix, then atomic rename
   - Readers see stale data until reload() is called (eventual consistency, not instant)
   - Integration with bd-3un.41 (staleness): staleness detector triggers reload()

2. Consistency Between Fast and Quality Indices:
   - CRITICAL: fast and quality indices MUST share the same doc_id set
   - During incremental indexing: fast index is always updated; quality index may lag
   - has_quality HashMap tracks which doc_ids have quality embeddings
   - Documents without quality embeddings get skipped during Phase 1 blend
   - Consistency check at open(): verify doc_count matches, log WARN if mismatch

3. Memory Pressure:
   - Two memory-mapped indices (256d fast + 384d quality) for each data directory
   - For 100K docs: fast ~49MB + quality ~73MB = 122MB total (f16)
   - OnceLock prevents double-loading but also prevents releasing memory
   - Future: consider LRU eviction for multi-directory deployments
   - Document memory requirements in INFO log at open()

4. File Locking:
   - Use advisory file locks (flock) during write operations
   - Readers do not lock (mmap provides read isolation)
   - Writer holds exclusive lock during rebuild, released on commit
   - Stale lock detection: check lock age, warn if > 5 minutes

5. Error Recovery:
   - Missing quality index: degrade to fast-only mode (not an error)
   - Corrupted fast index: return SearchError::IndexError, log ERROR
   - Partial write (crash during rebuild): .tmp files cleaned up on next open()

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
CRITICAL PATH: This is the single most important component. The TwoTierSearcher is what consumers interact with. It must be:

1. EASY TO USE: One-liner setup with auto-detection
2. CORRECT: Iterator contract must be exact (Initial → Refined → done)
3. FAST: Phase 0 must complete in < 15ms
4. RESILIENT: Quality failure → graceful degradation to fast results
5. COMPOSABLE: Optional lexical index, optional reranker

The iterator pattern is the key innovation — it lets callers process each phase independently:
- TUI: display fast results, then animate ranking changes
- HTTP API: return fast results, stream refinements via SSE
- CLI: print fast results, then update display
- Batch: just collect all phases

The blend factor of 0.7 (70% quality, 30% fast) was empirically chosen. Too high and fast rankings are ignored; too low and quality model adds little value. 0.7 is the sweet spot where quality dominates but fast provides a useful prior that smooths rankings.

comments.text:
ARCHITECTURE NOTE: Lexical Search Integration Across Crate Boundaries

The TwoTierSearcher lives in frankensearch-fusion. It needs to call lexical search
(Tantivy) for hybrid mode. But Tantivy is in frankensearch-lexical behind the
`lexical` feature flag. This creates a cross-crate integration challenge.

SOLUTION: Optional crate dependency with conditional compilation.

In frankensearch-fusion/Cargo.toml:
  [dependencies]
  frankensearch-lexical = { path = "../frankensearch-lexical", optional = true }

  [features]
  lexical = ["frankensearch-lexical"]

In TwoTierSearcher:
  #[cfg(feature = "lexical")]
  use frankensearch_lexical::LexicalIndex;

  pub struct TwoTierSearcher {
      // ...
      #[cfg(feature = "lexical")]
      lexical_index: Option<LexicalIndex>,
  }

When `lexical` feature is OFF:
  - TwoTierSearcher does semantic-only search (fast + quality, no RRF with lexical)
  - Phase 0: fast_embed -> fast_search -> yield Initial
  - Phase 1: quality_embed -> blend -> yield Refined
  - No Tantivy dependency compiled in

When `lexical` feature is ON:
  - TwoTierSearcher does hybrid search (semantic + lexical + RRF)
  - Phase 0: fast_embed -> fast_search -> lexical_search -> RRF fuse -> yield Initial
  - Phase 1: quality_embed -> blend -> re-fuse -> yield Refined

The facade (bd-3un.30) activates features based on consumer's Cargo.toml.
The consumer simply writes: frankensearch = { features = ["hybrid"] }
and gets both semantic and lexical automatically.

IMPORTANT: The auto() constructor must detect whether a Tantivy index exists
in data_dir and set lexical_index accordingly. If the lexical feature is enabled
but no Tantivy index exists, log WARN and proceed with semantic-only mode.

REVIEW FIX — async stream vs sync iterator, Phase 0 error handling, and canonical API:

1. SYNC ITERATOR vs ASYNC STREAM CONTRADICTION: The body describes a sync Iterator<Item = SearchPhase>. The asupersync revision says "NO sync iterators for the progressive protocol — use async stream or callback." These contradict.

   RESOLUTION: The progressive search API uses an async callback pattern (not Iterator, not Stream):

           &self,
           cx: &Cx,
           query: &str,

           on_phase: impl FnMut(SearchPhase) + Send,

2. OUTPUT TENSOR NAME FALLBACK: ONNX models use different output tensor names. Try in order: "logits", "output", "sentence_embedding". If none match, use the first output tensor by index. Reference: xf mxbai_reranker.rs has this fallback chain.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
CRITICAL IMPLEMENTATION NOTE: Sigmoid Activation

The raw ONNX output from cross-encoder models is a LOGIT, not a probability.
You MUST apply sigmoid activation: score = 1.0 / (1.0 + (-logit).exp())

Without sigmoid:
  - Logits range from roughly -10 to +10
  - Comparing raw logits between different query-doc pairs is meaningless
  - The reranker appears to work but produces garbage rankings

With sigmoid:
  - Scores range from 0.0 to 1.0
  - Scores are interpretable as P(relevant | query, document)
  - Rankings become meaningful and comparable

This was a real bug in the source codebase and must not be repeated.

Also: ONNX output tensor name varies by model:
  - "logits" (most common)
  - "output"
  - "sentence_embedding"
  - Fallback: first output tensor by index
Use a name fallback chain, not a hardcoded string.
